This approach provides a mathematical foundation for reflecting various features of the data and enables the creation of a single, versatile annotation that can be successfully trained on to achieve optimal classification results. Experimental findings based on datasets like CIFAR and MNIST highlight the effectiveness of this method in achieving better convergence and accuracy. Additionally, the paper demonstrates that this method can be used to detect and mitigate biases in machine learning models. Overall, the idea of universal annotation creation through delta lenses offers a novel mathematical model for designing this process and provides an innovative, robust, and highly adaptable method for tackling various real-world data challenges. Our presentation highlights the importance of finding steady-state solutions to the Boltzmann equation for low-density gas flow problems, particularly in the rarefied regime. Although it's challenging to obtain accurate numerical solutions in just a few cycles, we propose a novel iterative approach that combines an initial guess with the iterative application of the linearized collision operator, followed by a functional response. This method produces highly accurate results in as few as 40 iterations, matching the accuracy of venant-foster iterations, but with significantly fewer computations. To demonstrate its efficiency, we apply our method to a range of flow problems with various densities and surface conditions. Additionally, we create a publicly available code to facilitate future research and comparisons. Furthermore, we propose a new algorithm for creating rarefied flow databases based on the steady-state solution of the Boltzmann equation, enabling the creation of large databases in just a few hours. As a result, we can offer improved accuracy and significant reductions in cycle time for a wide range of flow problems in the database. Finally, we examine the limitations of our method, including its inability to accurately model flows that do not reach a steady-state in a few cycles, such as flows near surfaces or in the creation of vortices. To address this limitation, we propose the development of a bulk algorithm and a surface algorithm, but we have not yet completed this work in this presentation. Nevertheless, we have conducted initial research in this direction and look forward to continuing this research in the future. A related movie is available at https://uscmasim.github.io/BoltzmannIterativeMethod.

A key factor for online route navigation systems is effectively processing Transport Feed Specifications (TFS), a compact, structured format for describing trip information. However, the TFS format's accessibility is hindered due to its unique structure and vocabulary, making it challenging for laymen to decipher. To bridge this gap, this research aims to develop a TFS text-to-image translation method, a previously unexplored area. In exploring this approach, we encountered several obstacles. Firstly, there was a shortage of annotated TFS images to utilize supervised learning. Secondly, the TFS's complex route description, accompanied by limited contextual context, presented a significant obstacle for data interpretation. To address these issues, we devised a data enhancement strategy involving the repetition of TFS text paired with images, thereby generating substantial labeled TFS images. With this enlarged dataset, we employed a repetitive neural network model to propose an end-to-end TFS text-to-image translation framework, demonstrating its effectiveness through both objective and practical evaluations. We also introduced an interactive route visualization system, enabling users to conveniently locate destinations with the route information. The proposed system is currently available online at https://tfs-vis.github.io. Furthermore, the source code and annotated data can be accessed at github.com/Github4USF/TFS-VIS/ repository. We intend for this work to serve as a foundation and inspiration for future research. We are committed to making the system even more accessible and user-friendly in the future, with potential applications including 3D visualizations, route tracking, and other interactive systems. To improve learning from limited data, we develop an approach that enables us to acquire and store representative prototypes for each class. A key challenge lies in the absence of prior knowledge about these prototypes. Our method involves iteratively selecting and refining prototype candidates using cross-entropy loss and entropy reduction, ultimately leading to the extraction of more precise and representative prototypes. By integrating these prototypes into a model, we enhance our ability to reproduce the model's output even after the prototype exchange. As a result, this approach achieves robustness through the integration of human insight and automatic learning. We validate the efficacy of this framework in the context of semi-supervised few-shot learning, and our findings indicate substantial gains in performance over existing methods. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of this framework in additional scenarios such as self-supervised few-shot learning and stateless stateful models. You can find the accompanying code at https://github.com/Fuqiang_Chen/Fuqiang_Dissertation/blob/main/prototypes_for_fsl.pdf. 

The key contributions of our approach can be summarized as follows:

1.  We introduce a pioneering method for obtaining class-level prototypes in the context of few-shot learning.
2.  We adapt this and other techniques to various learning scenarios such as self-supervised few-shot learning and stateless stateful models.
3.  Our approach exhibits superior performance in comparison to established methods in the forms of tables and figures.

Two key applications of combinatorial optimization, the Set-Union Rucksack issue and the Budget-constrained Maximum Coverage Problem, have been linked to real-world problems through alternative formulations, with the former focusing on selecting items from a pack to maximize their value while adhering to a weight limit and the latter aiming to cover as many elements as possible from a set within a specified budget. Both problems require determining a subset of elements from a set of items, resulting in a rucksack analogy. While previous best-known solutions for these problems used exact methods with constraint programming or mixed-integer programming frameworks, our study demonstrates that simpler approaches can be developed by adapting existing techniques from related problems to both of these challenges with high performance results. Firstly, by adapting the Steiner point method for the rucksack format, a solution for both problems was devised, which yields an $\Omega(1.29^{k})$ factor for $k$ elements in a linear time complexity, with an $\mathcal{O}(k^2)$ preprocessing time requirement. Furthermore, a greedy solution for both problems was also developed, which yields an $\mathcal{O}(7/6)^k$ factor in a $\mathcal{O}(k)$ time complexity. Notably, our simple solutions even outperformed the best-known solution for the Budget-constrained Maximum Coverage Problem with a considerable improvement in runtime, while our solution for the Set-Union Rucksack issue results in a more compact formulation with increased readability and less dependency on third-party tools. In addition, our work has been applied to solve various real-world and theoretical problems. Specifically, our solution for the Budget-constrained Maximum Coverage Challenge with 100 elements and a budget of 80 successfully matched the state-of-the-art lower bound of 80.98% achieved using constraint programming. Our solution for the Maximum Coverage Challenge with 200 elements and a budget of 80 yielded a 81.00% coverage, which surpasses all other submitted solutions as of our knowledge cutoff in 2021. Our implemented solutions have been publicly released at https://github.com/PolimiOptimization/BMCP. Our work highlights that simple approaches, when thought-out and analyzed in-depth, can lead to high-performance results, which even outperform more complex methods in some cases. Our solutions have been awarded the BMAXX'21 Best Paper Award at the 21st Bi-Annual Workshop on Combinatorial Optimization at the University of Rome. Our work has also received the 2022 SILOXX

pause rates, statistical indicators, and the frequency of player actions.

To develop a context-aware and video-driven approach to identifying cyclists' risks, this research draws from mutual information theory, creating a quantitative measure that evaluates drivers' attention in different situations. Attention is modeled as a function of environmental factors and dynamically adjusted. A dynamic model of a driver's attention span is built, and a method for estimating attention is presented from surveillance video footage. For practical implementation, this approach is incorporated into a machine learning model, allowing the identification of cyclists' risk levels using traffic camera data. Our study focuses on three critical environments: intersections, pathways, and residential areas. The results show that our proposed model significantly outperforms existing benchmarks, achieving an impressive 91.3% accuracy on an actual road in Singapore. A comprehensive evaluation involving 15 scenarios reveals that the model's performance is greatly influenced by the speed of cyclists and drivers, the presence of pedestrians, and cyclists' use of helmets. This research lays the groundwork for a real-time cyclists' risk identification system, enabling informed interventions by public agencies, researchers, and individuals. A survey of 500 participants indicates that the model can be applied in a residential area provided that the speed limit is as low as 50 km/h. This study proposes a novel method for computing trajectory paths that can withstand disturbances and obstacles in complex environments with multiple obstacles. The suggested approach involves dividing the task into two sequential steps: first, identifying a protective barrier around the robot's intended destination; second, generating a collision-free path that ensures the robot stays within this safety margin. To achieve this, we utilize control barrier functions to define the barrier area and sample-based techniques to parameterize the path. The framework is exemplified through two of its applications - one involving a single robot avoiding multiple obstacles, and another simulating a cooperative robot mission where a group of robots work together to transport a package past a hazard, highlighting the efficacy of this concept in robotic teamwork. The presented methods are straightforward to implement using standard modeling tools like MATLAB and Casadi, making them easily adaptable in real-world robotic systems. To accelerate the learning process of model-free reinforcement learning agents, experience replay is highly effective. The standard approach of replaying experiences at random intervals can be inefficient, as it may not leverage the information contained in recent experiences. Recent studies have demonstrated that prioritized experience replay, which assigns higher priorities to experiences with larger rewards and updates more frequently, can accelerate learning. However, this method is often plagued by divergence issues, as updates to similar experiences can push them further away from their optimal targets. We have developed a new variational approach to experience replay, which assigns experiences to batches based on their proximity and updates them by minimizing the distance between them and their corresponding target distributions. This is achieved through a variational quadratic loss function, which is efficiently optimized using the conjugate gradient method. Our proposed algorithm, variance decrease, achieves convergence to optimal policy performance, as the target distribution varies, under certain conditions. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that variance decrease is a scalable and efficient method for experience replay. When compared to other reinforced learning baseline methods, it consistently achieves stable convergence and rapid learning across multiple environments, particularly in complex high-dimensional settings. Moreover, we have found that variance decrease can be used as a post-post optimization technique, as it can further improve model performance beyond that obtained through post optimization. Specifically, our proposed model, PPO-E, which combines PPO with variance decrease, is able to robustly generalize to multiple settings, as it reduces the impact of optimization by minimizing the variance of the policy gradient. Furthermore, variance decrease can be adapted for use in conjunction with other reinforced learning baseline methods, including Q-learning, as it can enhance its stability and robustness by reducing divergence. Our results also highlight the advantages of variance decrease when applied to learning in partially observable Markov decision processes. Overall, variance decrease represents a novel and efficient approach to experience replay, which can be used to accelerate learning and improve model generalizability across multiple settings. Future work may involve extending this method to accommodate changing reward functions, as well as its application in multiple settings. This research paper outlines a novel approach to the problem of preserving data lifetimes in Rust, utilizing its runtime interface to allocate and manage memory safely outside of Rust code. We integrate Rust with JavaScript, a language accommodating variable lifetime control, by creating a bridge connecting Rust and V8. Our solution, Josephine, permits direct access to the Rust heap, ensuring its visibility in JavaScript and facilitating its manipulation. Through a guaranteed interface, JavaScript can invoke Rust's drop method to deallocate memory on the Rust heap. This is complemented by a compiler pass that identifies and embeds rustc-generated type information within JavaScript compiled code, enabling runtime type checking by the JavaScript runtime. Our research demonstrates that, by leveraging multi-language programming, we can concurrently manage memory safety and performance considerations. Under standard conditions, amorphous materials like glass display a fracture strength several times greater than that of crystalline materials like ceramics. The reason for this disparity can be attributed to the pre-existing microscopic cracks present in glass, which reduces its fracture strength compared to perfectly smooth surfaces. In contrast, ceramics feature a uniform arrangement of atoms lacking in inherent defects. Initially assuming that the fracture strength of ceramics is infinite, accounting for potential defects only minimizes its fracture strength. The equilibrium fracture strength of crystalline materials, represented by the symbol σc, is primarily determined by the strength of chemical bonds within the material, denoted as σ0. The relationship between σc and σ0 yields σc = σ0 / √N, where N represents the total number of atoms surrounding each bond. For example, in the case of alumina (α-Al2O3), N equals 12. As a result, the equilibrium fracture strength of crystalline materials like alumina is characterized by the quantity 1 to 2 megapascals (MPa), a value significantly lower than that of amorphous materials such as glass, which possesses a fracture strength of around 100 MPa. The equilibrium fracture strength of materials like alumina is comparable to that of real ceramics, which explains why ceramic components rarely exhibit fracture damage after being used in applications like bearings or engine parts for an extended period of time. Conversely, the fracture of these materials typically occurs due to the initial cracks within the material. For decades, scientists have sought to understand the processes involved in the transportation of material and energy from an asteroid impact to Earth, particularly in the case of large impacts that result in massive tsunami waves. One such event is the Chelyabinsk incident in 2013, where a meteor burst released an astonishing amount of energy upon entering the atmosphere, resulting in a devastating explosion and a tsunami-like wave that traveled up to 30 meters in 30 microseconds. In the conventional wisdom regarding asteroid impacts, this phenomenon is attributed to the transfer of energy through shock waves and hydrodynamics. Yet, a comparable level of detail is required in the simulation of an asteroid impact's effects on the Earth's atmosphere and within the explosion itself, where the behavior of gases plays a crucial role. In our study, a novel approach for the simulation of an asteroid impact's effects on the Earth, specifically in the case of an exploding meteor, is presented by means of a simplified hydrodynamics model that effectively models and attributes the necessary properties to the participating materials within the explosion. This approach takes into account the properties of an exploding meteor's gas envelope, specifically those of a Type B cometoid, and resulting tidal waves that can travel numerous meters in a matter of milliseconds. By applying this model to a wide array of meteoroid types, it can be seen that the characteristics of an exploding meteor's gas envelope have a profound and substantial impact on the properties and behavior of a tidal wave that may potentially reach the viewer's location. Moreover, it is observed that the duration and intensity of a tidal wave that may reach the viewer's location vary directly with the size and properties of an exploding meteor, specifically those of a Type B cometoid. Interestingly, it is observed that the effects from an exploding meteor of this type, specifically those of a Mr. Bode's cometoid, may potentially result in a tidal wave with a significant duration and high intensity when viewed from a distance of 6-7 kilometers. The Fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly upgraded manufacturing processes within the industry by integrating the production planning process with practical production management systems. One major challenge faced during production planning revolves around handling uncertainty in processing times and machine capabilities, as well as dealing with uncertain sequence requirements and missing production instructions. Uncertainty in production sequences can be categorized into two primary types, namely, stochastic uncertainty, which is predictable in nature, and aleatoric uncertainty, which is random and unpredictable. Theoretical foundations of both types of uncertainties have been explored in the field of combinatorial optimization, although practical applications and solutions remain limited due to the interplay between these two uncertainties, making production planning a highly challenging task. This study aims to offer practical insights and solutions in addressing this challenge by developing novel uncertainties models compatible with real-world scenarios and employing these models to formulate the uncertain open-shop scheduling problem. A multi-objective linear program is proposed as a solution strategy to mitigate the effects of uncertainty in production sequences and processing times. The proposed model is empirically validated using actual production data sourced from a furniture manufacturing company and demonstrated to yield satisfactory results in representing both types of uncertainties and mitigating performance degradation. The proposed model has been successfully implemented in the planning department of the manufacturing company. A prominent method for safeguarding the location privacy of users involves obscuring their actual trace with an artificial one that matches their mobility pattern. Key factors in this process are the distance between consecutive real locations and the time between these locations. Current research typically focuses on the distance between locations, but in this paper, the time dimension is explored, with a specific analysis of the relationship between the artificial trace and the expected time it takes to travel between locations, known as the stochastic radius. We introduce a measure called LEP, which tracks the difference in location information based on the conditional expectation of the mobility model, and demonstrate that key properties of this measure are straightforward to compute. Building on this, we develop a privacy measure called LEPR, which combines LEP with the stochastic radius, and demonstrate its effectiveness using a concrete example. Furthermore, we establish a connection between LEPR and a well-known measure called the Fr\'echet distance by showing that LEPR can be seen as a form of generalized Fr\'echet distance. Based on this, we develop a method for constructing a privacy-preserving trace, and test the effectiveness of this method and the LEP and LEPR measures using real data sets and the LDOT mobility model. Our results show that LEPR provides better guarantees than LEP, and that both LEP and LEPR offer better protection than the stochastic radius. We also find that LEPR and the LEP and LEPR-based method are more effective than previously proposed methods. Additionally, we discuss the factors that affect the LEPR value and provide a method for improving the artificial trace to ensure better location privacy. We conclude by discussing future research opportunities prompted by these findings. Code-mixed speech representations face significant challenges due to their complex nature, where linguistic knowledge is required to interpret the code-mixed words as separate source language words. To tackle this issue, we introduce PESTO, a novel model for code-mixed speech recognition that uses transition points to create two distinct position-based representations. One representation captures code-mixed words as single units, while the other breaks them down into individual source language words. Our model leverages the flexibility of transformer architectures and contextual embeddings to enable PESTO to learn and incorporate this additional knowledge. Experimental results on code-mixed speech from Tamil-English and Hindi-English show that PESTO achieves notable improvements, with a 6.85% reduction in word error rate when compared to a baseline model using a single representation. Furthermore, PESTO outperforms a relevant neural network named CMLM by significant margins, with a reduction of 7.28% and 5.91% in word error rate in Tamil-English and Hindi-English datasets respectively. We have investigated how high-energy states near a van Hove singularity, specifically in the band structure of H$_3$S, affect its superconducting properties in relation to pressure. Utilizing a quasi-harmonic approximation, our analysis showed (at 50 GPa) that the heat capacity of H$_3$S exhibits a significant temperature variation at 230 K, just before reaching its critical temperature of 50.4 K. This result coincides with pressure-dependent computational findings from other sources. Notably, our calculations also indicated that high-energy states influence the critical temperature of H$_3$S at pressures below  I50 GPa, but have minimal effect at higher pressures (> 160 GPa). Conversely, our research shows that high-pressure conditions (> 160 GPa) have a pronounced adverse effect on the critical temperature of H$_3$S at low pressures (< 50 GPa), with the latter being more susceptible to external pressure due to the proximity of its Fermi level to a van Hove singularity. This specific feature is responsible for the distinct heat capacity characteristics observed in H$_3$S at 50 GPa and highlights its distinctiveness in comparison to other hydride superconductors. While the distinct heat capacity characteristics of H$_3$S at 50 GPa are indicative of its van Hoke singularity, they are absent in H$_{S+}$H at 160 GPa, where the Fermi level is far-removed from this critical point. Furthermore, our research shows that the critical temperature of H$_3$S is weakly responsive to external pressure at 50 GPa, but is highly sensitive in the 160 GPa regime, with the latter being characterized by a lower contribution of the electronic specific capacity to the total specific capacity in the superconducting state. This distinction highlights the distinct roles of the two charge carriers in the superconducting state at 160 GPa. Finally, our research shows that the critical temperature of H$_3$S at 50 GPa is weakly responsive to external pressure, in contrast to the distinct predictions made by the Herring-Volkov phenomenological model in the 160 GPa regime, where the superconducting state shows a substantial increase in response to increasing pressure. This result underscores the significant influence of the van Hove singularity on the superconducting properties of H$_3$H at 160 GPa. Mobile robots require flexible motion planning systems that can accommodate varying environments and object movements. To address this need, we propose a new approach using spatial separation obstacles to enable motion planning in dynamic environments. By selecting an obstacle set ensuring a feasible path exists for any configuration, we can develop an efficient motion planning system. However, determining an optimal obstacle set is a complex problem in general. To address this challenge, we identify a specific scenario – two robotic arms with a large working volume – where we can efficiently generate a suitable obstacle set. We also outline the limitations of our proposed method and directions for further research. Through high-quality video demonstrations and experimental results, we validate the efficacy of our approach. Additionally, we conduct a comparative analysis, demonstrating that our method outperforms existing motion planning techniques in terms of computational efficiency. The proposed method is available as an open-source system. To showcase its potential, we demonstrate its applications in multiple robotic scenarios. Moreover, we successfully implement and test this method on a two-armed robotic wheelchair system. We validate the performance of our system in a real-world environment, achieving the desired spatial separation without any complications. Overall, our method – spatial separation-based obstacles – offers a general and flexible framework for motion planning in diverse settings. We believe that our approach has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of dynamic motion planners. This research investigates the optimal method of encoding and user selection in massive MIMO networks through mid-tier caching, aiming to optimize a complex cost function related to network throughput, cache efficiency, and encoding complexity. By breaking down the problem into two distinct subproblems - user selection and encoding - we derive an algorithmic solution to tackle these issues. First, we formulate the user selection subproblem as a combinatorial optimization issue and translate it into an associated linear regression problem through the utilization of group LASSO variables. Secondly, we devise an algorithmic solution to the encoding subproblem by distinguishing between baseline and enhanced caching scenarios and deriving two distinct sets of regression equations to represent baseline and enhanced caching scenarios. Our proposed framework establishes a link between user selection and encoding, as well as between baseline and enhanced caching scenarios, through the use of group LASSO variables. Furthermore, we employ the Lasso algorithm and Stackelberg game to obtain the optimal solution to the user selection and encoding subproblems. To alleviate computational constraints, we first prove that Lasso solutions to the two sets of regression equations are stackable and apply the Cholesky decomposition. Next, we select a subset of Lasso solutions to the user selection subproblem through the sparsity property of Lasso solutions. Finally, we obtain the optimal solution to the encoding subproblem by multiplying the selected subspace matrices with the corresponding data matrices, thereby obtaining the solutions to the two subproblems. Our algorithmic solution, dubbed the Collaborative User Selection and Encoding Scheme via Group LASSO, enjoys the virtues of simplicity, low computational complexity, and high scalability, all while surpassing the baseline solution to the user selection and encoding subproblems. The Lasso algorithmic solution to the user selection subproblem is analyzed in terms of its optimal solution bounds and deterministic guarantees. The derived bounds are obtained by translating the Lasso optimization issue into an associated second-order cone optimization issue. Moreover, we establish the convergence properties of the Stackelberg game and the Lasso algorithmic solution to the encoding subproblem. Our system combines a Neuroevolutionary Platform for Automation and Robotics, or NEPAR. Our model consists of two interconnected modules: the Model Description Module, which explains the rules governing agent interactions, and the Model Execution Module, where the actual assembly process takes place. To train these agents efficiently, we've developed a specialized algorithm that mimics the rumelhart backpropagation method and introduced a new fitness function that calculates the geometric mean of multiple fitness measures to improve stability and versatility in assembly capabilities. Additionally, we've made the source code for NEPAR and our experiments available as open-access repositories under the GitHub platform. Our study's quantitative findings, displayed in a new benchmark called the NEPAR Benchmark, or NB, demonstrate that our model achieves comparable results to prior state-of-the-art self-assembling algorithms. Our study's data indicate that a more skilled agent not only contributes to more efficient assembly but also to increased resistance to disturbances of all kinds. Furthermore, we've observed that more accomplished agents exhibit a greater diversity of techniques to perform tasks, which in turn enhances their ability to adapt to a wide range of scenarios. These outcomes as a whole underscore the significance of investigating the interplay between generalization and efficiency in assembly processes. Ultimately, the results of our study validate that with sufficient data, complex tasks can be mastered by agents even when the underlying rules governing their interactions are not fully understood. In order to enhance supervised Graph Neural Network training with limited labeled data, we propose an iterative method that integrates semi-supervised and semi-self-supervised learning. The first stage involves standard semi-supervised learning techniques to expand the labeled set. The second stage uses a self-supervised loss to refine the model's predictions on the expanded set. Regularly reapplying this method converges towards a state where the model makes optimal use of all available data, with each iteration improving prediction accuracy on the initially labeled nodes. Additionally, we introduce a new loss function for self-supervised learning that focuses on nodes with inaccurate predictions, enhancing overall prediction accuracy. The analytical proof of this method's convergence, as well as empirical validation on both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrates its effectiveness when working under data scarcity conditions. Research into radio-frequency breakdown and experimental settings for the AWAKE experiment at CEA-Saclay involves modeling the interaction between the accelerated particles and the wakefield using a combined framework consisting of three-dimensional and one-dimensional codes. Specifically, the enhanced radiation produced by the wakefield's amplitude gradient in plasma has been directly observed in experiments. Furthermore, the increased proton acceleration achieved in proton-driven plasma wakefield acceleration can lead to increased betatron radiation, thus serving as a viable diagnostic tool. Based on a comparison with 2020 measurements at the AWAKE experiment, our simulation results yield an estimated 100 million times lower radiation threshold for detecting the betatron radiation, corresponding to a single-shot measurement. We have also analyzed the effects of experimental parameters such as seeding electron density, proton beam energy, and electron injection location on radio-frequency breakdown and betatron radiation. Our findings suggest that in certain configurations with correct electron injection, reduced radiation coupling could delay the occurrence of RF breakdown. We have further estimated the detectability limits of betatron radiation for future experiments with increased particle accelerators, finding that in some settings, radiation from the betatron "island" may become undetectable. We have also explored potential applications for using betatron radiation in future experiments on both heavy ion collisions and the transverse proton beam modulation experiments at the ENS facility in France. By considering these future research goals, our simulation results demonstrate that in some scenarios, the enhanced betatron radiation may become a significant issue in terms of its potential to interfere with precision physics experiments, whereas in other scenarios, the increased radiation may become a valuable asset in experiments involving beam modulation. The theoretical and computational framework developed in this study is expected to contribute significantly to a broader range of research goals in accelerated physics, wherein the accelerated particles are either injected into the wakefield by an external radio frequency signal or by a separate ionized beam. In particular, our simulation results indicate that in settings where the accelerated beam is injected into a separate wakefield generated by a nitrogen laser, the enhanced radiation produced by the wakefield's phase-space "island" is significantly reduced. In contrast, our simulation results also suggest that in settings where the accelerated particles are either injected into a separate wakefield generated by a high-power microwave, the enhanced radiation produced by the wakefield's phase-space "island" is significantly increased. In contrast, a certain high-spin hyperon is essential in producing Sigma particles. The primary function of a headline in any news article is to captivate the reader, drawing them in by summarizing the main content in a concise and intriguing manner. With growing interest in large language models like BERT, the task of generating headlines automatically has become increasingly feasible. In this research, we focus on assessing the effectiveness of generated headlines rather than their origin. To evaluate the plausibility of headlines, we introduce a straightforward metric that estimates the average understanding of the sentence by a typical reader, leveraging the knowledge of reading levels as a benchmark. Through our analysis, we examine the impact of various factors on the viability of headlines. Moreover, we demonstrate that a fine-tuned BERT model can be trained to identify genuine headlines with remarkable accuracy. By comparing our results with those obtained from human evaluations of the H3: There Is No Central Bank dataset, we find evidence supporting the reliability of reading-level-based metrics for assessing the credibility of LLM-generated content. Ultimately, we explore the potential applications of our proposed metric and future research directions. The code and models used in our research are publicly available at https://github.com/jaykim2018/HeadlineVerification.

Future large-scale radio interferometers, such as the Square Kilometer Array, will incur significant costs due to the precision required for their antenna location and vector measurements. Current accurate methods result in a quadratic cost barrier, necessitating new search strategies to minimize these expenses. In this paper, we examine techniques for optimizing the processing time and number of vector measurements for these interferometers, based on their relative sky images and with consideration of their significance to the science community. By integrating data from multiple antennas and calculating local correlation values, we maximize the information gained from each measurement while reducing the processing time. These strategies can be applied dynamically as the sky images change over time. Compared to existing methods, our approach yields substantial cost reductions, scaling linearly with the number of antennas and varying inversely with the number of factors being measured. Simulation results indicate a significant reduction of around two orders of magnitude. Additionally, we observe that by leveraging the radiometric hypothesis, our approach can take full advantage of the system's capabilities, leading to substantial improvements in sensitivity and the detection of rare events. Notably, we estimate this optimization could reduce the required number of vector measurements by a factor of twenty to one hundred when scanning the entire sky. These strategies, inspired by the sparse recovery algorithm, use a modified version of the Rubin Visible Object Detection pipeline and can be integrated into the existing processing chain. Our algorithm can be executed on graphics processing units and yields excellent results, likely expandable to other scanning strategies such as row-by-row scanning with minimal modifications. Ultimately, these optimized strategies could minimize the computational and hardware expenses of large-scale interferometers, potentially leading to significant cost reductions of the kind seen in the Square Kilometer Array Prototype. The fundamental of diversification is crucial for optimizing investment returns over time and reducing risk. However, with the rise of alternative pure play investment products, achieving a diversified portfolio has become increasingly complex. This research uses generative adversarial networks (GANs) to develop a method for simulating and optimizing portfolios in the alternative space. In particular, we focus on the sample selection bias problem and propose an autoencoding conditional GAN model that generates synthetic transaction data. Our approach is demonstrated through an examination of the hybrid exchange-traded fund and alternative beta products spaces, utilizing historical data from the Global X Hybrid ETF to ensure statistical significance. By incorporating this model into a reinforcement learning agent, we can obtain a more informed perspective on the cost of hedging different investment strategies. Our results show that incorporating alternative investments can lower the risk-equivalent cost by 15% to 65%, depending on the specific investment composition. This highlights the potential benefits of alternative investments for investors seeking to optimize their portfolio's performance. Furthermore, we address the challenge of data scarcity often associated with alternative assets through the deployment of our Autoencoding Conditional GAN model. This enables us to generate synthetic data and thereby circumvent the limitations of limited data availability. Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of the space of hybrid exchange-traded funds and alternative beta products, providing valuable insights for investors and further establishing the link between alternative investments and risk-efficient investment strategies. Finally, to promote future research, we make the code and data available for reference. The contribution of our work can be summarized as follows:  From a methodological perspective, we introduce the concept of autoencoding conditional GAN for simulating and optimizing investment returns in the alternative space. The use of conditional GANs allows us to incorporate fundamental portfolio optimization criteria into the generated synthetic data. Autoencoders, on the other hand, are particularly useful in managing fund liquidation scenarios. This contribution represents the first time such a technique has been applied to alternative investment spaces.  From a empirical perspective, we examine the sample selection bias problem in the alternative space and assess its financial impact on investment costs for pure-play and hybrid ETFs. The results show that incorporating alternative investments can significantly lower investment costs for investors.  From a practical perspective, we provide investors with actionable and detailed information on the benefits and risks associated with different investment strategies, taking into account their specific objectives and constraints. This study investigates the challenges and opportunities related to creating accessible content on social media. Through a survey of 292 individuals with visual impairments and low vision, we gleaned insights from their experiences with accessible content creation, alongside identifying the key obstacles and the level of support required from social media companies to facilitate greater user involvement. The findings suggest that social media companies play a crucial role in addressing these challenges, highlighting opportunities for innovation and collaboration to enhance accessibility. Ultimately, our research seeks to contribute valuable user voices to the development of accessible digital platforms. 

The key obstacles in creating accessible content on social media include:

1. Inadequate accessibility features and user-friendly interfaces.
2. Insufficient accessibility training and support for users and service providers.
3. Concerns over feedback and the impact of user reporting on account suspension.

The key opportunities for innovation and collaboration on social media accessibility include:

1. Developing more effective and accessible content creation tools.
2. Improving communication and feedback loops between users and service providers.
3. Increasing the training and education of users and content moderators on accessibility.

1. Integration of assistive technology that better supports visual access and mobility.

This work concerns parabolic variants of complex Monge-Ampere and Hessian equations, with a focus on establishing $L^{\infty}$ a priori estimates. Under specified boundary and geometric constraints, we demonstrate that the Monge-Ampere equation admits an $L^\infty$ bound, yielding a local parabolic Hormander type theorem. In the case of generalized Hessian equations described by Phong-Tam-Si-Dinh, similar estimates are achieved, provided the boundary has a sufficiently high degree. Furthermore, in the context of the extended Monge-Ampere equation encompassing all log-concave metrics at infinity, we discover that additional geometric constraints are required to obtain an $L^\infty$ bound. This investigation heavily draws upon findings from previous studies on elliptic equations as well as those regarding the geometric constraints on plurisicative regions, encompassing all log-concave metrics at infinity. Moreover, it appears that the assumptions related to metrics at infinity are the natural requirements for parabolic stability as they were for the elliptic case, as evidenced by the behavior of the equations under rescaling in both the parabolic and static contexts. Consequently, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of the precise assumptions needed for parabolic stability, depending on whether a metric has an infinite boundary or is bounded by an affine segment. We've established a new method to determine which properties of functions are preserved when restricting the lambda-calculus to its typed components. This method also allows us to pinpoint the exact limitations of conversion principles within certain typed lambda-calculus frameworks. By utilizing this approach, we've successfully identified specific conditions under which certain conversion principles are valid or invalid in various contexts. To further explore the concept, we've introduced a new definition for well-typed substitution, allowing us to assess the validity of substitution principles within certain types-based lambda-calculus systems. This definition also provides a basis for comparing the computational power of different typed lambda-calculus systems by categorizing them according to specific criteria. We've demonstrated that many standard calculi preserve a significant property of functions, while some other structures are too permissive and can accommodate a wide range of functions. This work also raises fundamental questions about the nature of typing as a means to achieve closure under composition. Specifically, we've shown that certain typed lambda-calculus systems that are otherwise well-behaved fail when attempting to include primitive recursion. This phenomenon suggests that certain forms of recursion are inherently untypable. We've successfully identified efficient algorithms to determine whether a given function is within the scope of many standard lambda-calculus systems that we've previously defined. These algorithms not only provide a positive answer but also can compute a corresponding function within those systems when the input value satisfies a certain condition. We've achieved this result by employing a technique known as "negative translation." Given a set S and a function that assigns a value to its elements, this note outlines a procedure to construct a matroid consisting of subsets with desirable properties. This process is then applied using a specific function that derives from first-order logic, resulting in the attainment of a well-known matroid, the outer algebra. Utilizing this approach, we either prove or conjecture the non-existence of a matroid having certain properties: for each property P, either we can construct a matroid satisfying the next property, or we can construct a matroid satisfying the previous property. Consequences of this include the non-existence of a matroid in which mono-hereditary and antimonotone properties coincide, and the non-existence of a matroid such that for every given level, there exists a mono-hereditary property at that level. Furthermore, we can construct a matroid consisting of subsets with descending sets of a particular length, resulting in the outer algebra matroid, and we can construct a matroid consisting of subsets with upsets not exceeding a particular level, also resulting in the outer algebra matroid. This process can be generalized using a specific function that assigns a value to the elements of a set S. One of the main points is that the outer algebra has an almost universal property: for any matroid property having a finite definition, if the property is hereditary, then the outer algebra also has this property, and this result holds for corresponding levelized properties as well. This generalization can be applied to consecutive matroid properties as well, resulting in the outer algebra. One of the main open problems is to construct a matroid property such that the outer algebra has the preceding property, but not the following property. This problem is particularly significant in the case of mono-hereditary properties and upset properties. As social media grows in popularity, the ease with which anonymous accounts can be created has led to an increase in abusive content, including hate speech. A key challenge in addressing hate speech is the difficulty of accurately identifying it, particularly given the varied and innovative language used by authors. Additionally, factors such as grammatical errors and regional dialects complicate the process. A recent method developed by Li et al. employs attention mechanisms to consider the whole text when making predictions, and incorporates linguistic knowledge to guide the modeling process. In contrast, human reviewers rely on the textual and contextual information available to make an informed decision. An improved method is proposed in this paper, which mimics human decision-making by incorporating contextual information and employing a dual-task training framework to enhance the consideration of individual words. The method achieves this by using word-level representations to guide the hate speech detection process. The hate360 dataset is utilized in this research, which includes numerous social media platforms and 800,000 annotated sentences. The experiment demonstrates that the proposed method performs favorably when compared with the original Li et al.'s method and several other baseline models. Notably, when Li et al.'s method is tested on datasets other than their own, it yields disappointing results. The method's effectiveness is highlighted through the presentation of several case studies that illustrate its capacity to utilize contextual information. The Sun is thought to have a superdense core containing neutrons, which some researchers believe could be accessible to experimenters in the near future. This theory suggests that neutron-rich isotopes decay into the neutron-rich isotones by releasing an electron, a process known as the proton process, and this decay rate varies depending on the interior of the Sun. By searching for this variation in the Sun's core using the Internet-based Axion Resonant Characteristic Curves experiment's modified version, researchers can determine the value of the proton decay life span. This modified version, BabyIAXO, has a reduced number of magnets but maintains high detection sensitivity. If detected, a significant variation would imply the presence of neutrons in the Sun's core. This investigation, conducted by BabyIAXO, would be the first to detect the proton decay in the Sun, providing the most compelling evidence for the neutron-rich isotones and significantly advancing our understanding of the Sun's core. This discovery could also have far-reaching implications for the understanding of dense stellar cores and dense matter. This topic will be thoroughly discussed at the XXXIX Meeting of the Italian Physical Society in June 2021.

In the limit of equilibrium, this system reduces to a well-known model of the predator-prey type. It is also shown that this model reduces to a well-known model at equilibrium along with various other well-known models under specific limit conditions. Ecosystem models relying on Fickian diffusion for resource movement are straightforward and computationally efficient, yet there is evidence that this approach doesn't accurately reflect environmental processes, especially in arid regions. Our research investigates the effects of non-local foraging on vegetation patterns developing in arid environments. We enhanced existing models by replacing diffusion with Laplace dynamics for resource movement, allowing plants to detect and respond to their environment in a non-local manner. Our results demonstrate that different Laplace-based movement rules produce stable and unstable outcomes, with the Laplace model often resulting in the disappearance of resource or plants. A fundamental requirement for various Advanced Manufacturing processes is process registration, which ensures accurate registration of a tool moving within a specific workspace limitations. We developed an approach for registering a KINO robot structure with consideration for collisions and constraints. Our method allows real-time modification of robot path segments to maintain within viable workspace areas. To accelerate this process, we utilized the uniform bicompact mapping framework. With this method, the tool's registration can be completed within 1 second and optimized for faster and more efficient processing. The results show that our tool's path average speed increase to 90% of its initial path length and the number of modified path segments is significantly reduced, thereby enabling much faster processing times for overall robot system. Deducing statistical inference results, which often involves drawing conclusions outside of a hypothesis testing framework, has practical applications that go beyond standard hypothesis testing outcomes. In contrast to testing, deduction requires that findings be consistent with any given data and is particularly significant in frequentist theories of inference. Until recently, it was unclear whether deduction was feasible for some statistical metrics. This study demonstrates that deduction is possible for Kendall's tau rank correlation metric. Furthermore, we establish that for large sample sizes, conventional confidence intervals for Kendall's tau will also serve as valid deductive intervals, highlighting their broader applicability. We provide real-world examples to illustrate the distinction between testing and deduction, as well as the sample size requirement for the latter. Finally, we illustrate the implementation of the deduction method in a Bayesian framework for Kendall's tau using posterior intervals. This study also identifies an important open question regarding large-sample deductive intervals that remains unanswered. This contribution expands upon a presentation at the IIASA workshop on large-scale optimization in Schliersee, Germany, in 2018. The initial paper in this series provided an overview of IIASA's Aspect Pivot Simplex (APS) project, which aims to improve efficiency in computing optimal values for linear programs by leveraging structural information obtained during the initial phase of the simplex method. In particular, APS introduces a variant of the simplex algorithm that exploits the lower-boundedness of decision variables to iteratively refine a feasible direction until it reaches a singular limit, at which point the algorithm transitions to using numerical methods for direction computation, utilizing two-sided linearization. This paper demonstrates that, in the absence of correlative uncertainty, the APS method can achieve a linear iteration bound, thereby establishing a theoretical efficiency limit. The APS code has been extensively tested on numerous problems from various fields, showcasing its potential for significant speedup compared to classical implementations of the simplex algorithm. The proposed method also offers a flexible and adaptable framework for handling various computational requirements. A comprehensive evaluation has been included to illustrate the method's feasibility and computational benefits. The presented results are informed by IIAS's extensive experience in optimizing large-scale linear programs for energy-related applications and problems with variable lower bounds due to external constraints. A detailed comparison with the most widely used commercial linear programming solver, GUSSXLP, has been conducted to illustrate the computational advantages of the APS method in terms of iteration count and solution time. The reasons behind the outperformance of the APS method, even in scenarios where variable lower bounds are not directly applicable, have been discussed. This phenomenon can be observed in two distinct spectral lines, at -24.7 km/s and -35.9 km/s, which are 24 km/s and 35 km/s away from the H II region's frequency peak. Using a 3D radiative transfer code to investigate these emissions, we discover that they arise from two adjacent neutral hydrogen layers, approximately 1 pc thick, at the boundary between the H II region and the interstellar medium. The emissions from these diffuse gas slabs outshine those from the H II region when observed at very low frequencies and have potential to be used as indicators for similar neutral hydrogen layers elsewhere. Our observation that the HI emissions from the H II region are weaker than expected can be accounted for by incorporating the effects of radiative absorption on the HI gas within the region. In the 1970s, the $\beta$-particle emission theory posed a puzzle that cannot be resolved using steady beta transfers, as it resulted in a contradiction with the conservation of energy. The resolution to this problem led to the development of the $\beta$-transfers concept, which posits that beta decays occur through a series of two-step processes. We propose an additional type of $\beta$-transfers, called greedy $\beta$-transfers, where the initial neutron or proton emission is followed by a significant gap in the mass number $0\le\delta\le2$. The feasibility of detecting these ambitious $\beta$-transfers is evaluated across their entire range of possible mass differences. Our investigation suggests that future experiments using highly precise mass spectrometers may be capable of observing these ambitious $\beta$-transfers with relatively low effort in laboratories where the production of rare isotopes is already being pursued. If detected, these ambitious $\beta$-transfers could have a substantial impact on our understanding of both the atomic and nuclear levels. Additionally, we have computed the emission strengths required for experimental detection that could be achieved using existing facilities such as CSRIBL II, ISOLDE, and FRIB. The results of our investigation indicate that sub-percent measurements of $\delta$ gaps may be within the reach of future facilities such as FRIB. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a better comprehension of the complex and dynamic interplay between the atomic and nuclear levels. Deep Learning models are typically classified into two groups based on parameter variability: 
  1) models with fixed parameter values (like fully-connected networks), where the model is trained to determine parameter values; 
  2) models with parameter values that rely on the size of the input (like Neural Turing machines), where the model is either fixed and its parameter values are determined by the size of the input or part of a larger model whose parameter values are known). 
  We developed a graph neural network (GNN) interpreter that can take into account the size of the graphs and modify its parameters accordingly. The proposed GNN interpreter is applicable to a wide range of models that rely on the size of the input. 
  We have adapted the PyTorch~GNN library to make the GNN interpreter available for the evaluation of how much a model's performance changes in response to variations in network size. 
  We have applied the proposed GNN interpreter to various benchmark tasks and studies in order to understand the behavior of neural networks in response to variations in network size. 
  A theoretical scaling law for deep and noisy models has been discovered on benchmark tasks. 
  It was also observed that Leaky Relu activation function causes perturbations in the input to be forgotten at an exponential rate that is inversely proportional to the length of the network memory. 
  The proposed GNN interpreter allows the creation of inverse models that are linear in size, have no cyclic dependencies, and are highly efficient, with a cost ratio of linearly varying model performance and actual model performance ranging from 0.70 to 0.95. 
  It was also found that the size of the input and the number of samples should should be should be maximized in order to understand the behavior of neural networks in response to variations in network size. 
  Several of the above findings were also validated using Amoeba, an optimization algorithm that is linear in size, has no cyclic dependencies, and is highly efficient. 
  It was also found that the size of the input should should be maximized in order to understand the behavior of neural networks in response to variations in network size. 
  A potential future work that is investigated in this document is the creation of a tool that can take into account the behavior of neural networks in response to variations in network size in order to improve the efficiency of the evaluation of neural networks.

another through a series of reciprocal tasks. The results show that when
individuals are permitted to choose their partners and acquire knowledge at
their own pace, the language tends to evolve towards consistency. The
convergence of vocabulary items to specific meanings occurs as the system
reaches a state of equilibrium. The length and dynamics of this convergence
are significantly influenced by the degree of variability in word associations,
inconsistent usage that is widespread, and the dynamic nature of social
connections. The presented model is versatile, implying its potential for
applicability to diverse fields of study. The implications of this study are
further explored in the context of practical applications, such as collective
knowledge acquisition processes. The results reveal that social connections,
influenced by linguistic compatibility, can serve as an essential factor in

key components of establishing effective and harmonious communication systems.

The problem seeks to find the minimax norm $\|f\|_2^2$ among all functions $f \in {\bf F}_S$ that satisfy ${\bf M}f = f$ within a given frequency band. The function $f$ here represents an ${\bf R}^d$-valued vector. We establish that the above problem lacks a solution if $d \geq 2$ and determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of the solution in form of a matrix inequality. This condition is related to the invertibility of a specific block-diagonal matrix. The same problem for the combination of rank-one transfer functions reveals similar outcomes. We prove that the corresponding minimax norm either does not exist or is infinite, with exact criteria for its existence or finiteness defined by a specific matrix inequality involving block-diagonal matrices. The same matrix inequality applies to the combination of translates rank-$rank \ell$ vectors. The use of Li-6 in dark matter searches offers a new option for the direct detection of spin-tracery interactions. We've conducted a study to see how improvements in detector sensitivity will affect the ability to detect certain dark matter interactions, specifically on the proton, neutron, and the electron-nucleus combination, by utilizing Li-6's nuclear mass splitting. We've taken into account both the nuclear structure factors and the Earth's velocity-dependent corrections. We found that the electron-nucleus combination has a significant impact on the detection sensitivity, while the velocity-dependent interactions are more likely to be detected in Li-6 than in Xenon. Our study suggests that future Li-6 experiments could be able to detect certain dark matter interactions that are currently beyond reach with Xenon. We've used a range of assumptions about the dark matter cross-sections and mass ranges, and our study represents a first comprehensive investigation of the potential for Li-6 to be used in direct dark matter searches, particularly for spin-dependent interactions. Our main finding is that the combination of Li-6's mass splitting and its electron-nucleus combination factor makes future Li-6 experiments potentially more sensitive to dark matter than Xenon for a range of assumed parameters. A novel low-level vision task known as blind image restoration is investigated in this study. Specifically, we focus on repairng both damage and noise affecting images. Traditional approaches typically assume a single filter or noise pattern across the entire image. However, the problem we're addressing exhibits inherent variability in filter patterns, making single-model approaches inadequate. Building on the success of kernel-based methods in handling variability, we introduce the kernel mixture model (KMM), which consists of multiple kernel functions combined with unknown weighting factors. By representing restorable effects as the convolution of images and weighting factors, the problem is transformed into estimating the kernel parameters and weighting factors. To achieve this, we've developed an end-to-end, differentiable network called KMMNet, incorporating a module that expands the receptive field to effectively apply kernel models to large-scale images. KMMNet is trained based on the expectation-maximization algorithm and can be optimized using stochastic gradient descent, making it a highly effective solution for various blind image restoration tasks. To further validate our method, we've created a new dataset, CSF+SN, to study the effects of computer simulations and human eyes on image degradation. Our experiments compare KMMNet with numerous state-of-the-art, single-model approaches and demonstrate its superiority in restoring images free from noise and damage. Additionally, our study is also conducted with other prominent datasets, including dehazing and self-casting tasks, where KMMNet shows its robustness and efficiency in handling various types of image degradation. Our related code and dataset are available at https://github.com/whwu1024/Blind_image_restoration_KMMNet. With these contributions, our study opens up a new research direction for handling inherent variability in image degradation and paves the way for further research on multi-variance in image degradation and restoration. At the same time, our study also sheds light on the effects of computer simulations and human eyes on image degradation and restoration. Moreover, our study highlights the significance of the kernel model in handling inherent variability in blind image restoration. Experimental results show that UPS$^2$ accelerates GNN model design at a 25.6% rate on real-world graph datasets, such as Amazon, YouTube, and Wikipedia, and outperforms 11 state-of-the-art GNN models by 5.14% on edge prediction and 4.25% on node prediction. Several techniques have been suggested to privately release a low-rank low-dimensional matrix while preventing the disclosure of underlying column-specific facts, such as row spans and column pairs. This paper builds upon the findings of previous DP low-rank matrix estimation research, distilling its key insights into a set of fundamental principles - which we label the 'Huber axioms. We contend that any differential privacy-friendly approach to estimating a low-rank matrix must adhere to these principles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fulfilling the Huber axioms enables the creation of stable and robust methods for protecting data privacy, and that such methods are provably just as effective as non-private methods, which is particularly the case in accordance with the 'price of anocracy' - a phenomenon where the degradation in quality resulting from differential privacy implementation is directly proportional to $\chi^2(m,r)=$ O($r^2$). To validate the Huber axioms, we provide two independent proofs, one of which is derived from the findings of an existing study. Using the findings from an experimental analysis, we show that the degradation in quality resulting from the implementation of differential privacy is directly proportional to $\chi^2(m,r)=$ O($r^2$). The capabilities of Neural Machine Translation models can be enhanced using data augmentation methods such as CSIA. However, since CSIA involves translating a single sentence from one language to another, maintaining the original sentence's meaning can be challenging, particularly when dealing with ambiguous words that have different meanings in two languages. To address this issue, we propose a new CSIA approach that uses lexical substitutions to find equivalent words in the target language. Our approach specifically takes into account the contextual aspects that affect a word's meaning during a code-switching process. We employed a BERT-based model to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method in comparing the meanings of CS and monolingual words. Hexahedral mesh topologies are widely applied in the fields of engineering and scientific research. In contrast to the well-understood characteristics of tetrahedral meshes, those of hexahedral meshes are often obscure, leading people to believe that uniform refinement of hexahedral meshes, when possible, preserves their advantages. However, this assumption is incorrect as periodic hexahedral mesh refinement leads to mesh degradation. In this research, we demonstrate that when hexahedral mesh refinement is feasible, up to 58 different types of hexahedral mesh topologies can be created from a given one. We define and categorize these new topologies based on their orientation patterns and how the hexahedra are arranged. Additionally, this study provides a detailed evaluation of hexahedral mesh quality using criteria such as point quality, edge length ratios, and dihedral angles. We employ a point-set method to generate hexahedral meshes that are initially high-quality and retain their high quality even after various refinements. In this research, the Advection-Diffusion solver, the Harlow-Brown solver, and the Langberg-Lane solver are used to test the meshes generated. These solvers simulate numerical methods' effects and measure how the hexahedral meshes' high quality is maintained up to 16 and 32 refinements. We conduct an approachable analysis of hexahedral mesh topologies based on their persistence in arrangement, a concept related to the simplicial complex preserving property. We discuss the potential applications of this research in mesh-based solvers and the need for further studies to uncover more category 3, 4, and 5 hexahedral mesh topologies. The research highlights that more than 160 hexahedral mesh topologies might exist, and identifying them all could greatly contribute to the development of hexahedral mesh-based solvers. The research's findings and results are displayed through visualizations and documented in detailed images. Research has established that the ventral temporal cortex plays a pivotal role in this process but the specific mechanisms involved are still unclear. In this paper, a deep neural network is proposed to model the animacy arrangement process by building on existing multi-layered neural networks that have been trained to recognize animal and vehicle images. By integrating these networks into a two-part system, our model effectively differentiates between animacy categories and sub-categories, mirroring behavioral observations from humans. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the lower layers of this dual system are more sensitive to animacy sub-categories while the upper layers are more sensitive to animacy categories, achieving correct classification of animal and vehicle images 90% of the time when given partial image information from lower layers or when given full image information across all layers. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the animacy arrangement process is shaped by both image information and prior knowledge, and that prior knowledge has a greater impact on the classification process at the sub-category level than at the category level, especially for difficult image segments that require more computational power to decode. Overall, our findings provide essential insights into the underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex arrangement system. If validated by future experiments, our model has the potential to be deployed in various fields such as robotics. Our analysis is based on a large-scale visual understanding database consisting of 2.2 million images spanning 2,000 different animal and vehicle classes, and its analysis reveals that the animacy arrangement system is more effective at higher levels of image complexity, and that prior knowledge has a greater impact on the classification process at the sub-category level than at the category level. This paper investigates the convergence speeds in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem utilizing spectral metrics. We derive sharp bounds on the operator norm and spectral measure convergence rates for ergodic ergodicity constants. We also establish that a measure-preserving ergodic system with slow ergodicity has a spectral measure convergence rate comparable to $\frac{1}{\log^2 t}$. A key aspect of our findings involves examining the efficacy of a particular method in achieving uniform convergence across various ergodicity constants. We further extend our research to cover non-ergodic systems, covering weighted ergodic transformations and certain dynamical systems on probability spaces. In addition, a note is provided at the end to confirm the universality of ergodicity constants for measure-preserving ergodic systems. The universal nature of these constants was initially demonstrated by P. Szegö. A similar concept was later explored by P. Billings and P. Montgomery in their publication on ergodicity constants for $l^p$-spaces. Our research on this topic is documented in the publication by P. Billings, P. Montgomery, and M. P. Vraciu. The current text specifically examines the ergodicity constants for measure-preserving ergodic systems. Our research further identifies the ergodicity constants for certain dynamical systems as well as the rate of spectral measure convergence in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for certain cases. The text specifically examines the model $\{T_t\}$ of one-dimensional simple harmonic motion. Our research shows that the rate of spectral measure convergence in this model is $\frac{1}{\log^2 t}$. This finding contrasts with the rate of $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ obtained in the publication by J. B. Miller. The current text identifies the ergodicity constant for the model $\{T_t\}$ as $|T_t(x)-x|$ with $x\in [0,1]$. This finding confirms a previous conjecture of P. Szegö. Our research further establishes that the rate of spectral measure convergence in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for the model $\{T_t\}$ is contingent on the value of $|T_t(x)-x|$. Galaxy clusters serve as key indicators for self-interacting dark matter.  A phenomenon called gravitational lensing can provide insights into the interactions between dark matter particles, especially through their impact on minor collisions between smaller and larger halos.  This process has been primarily studied using simulations of major interactions between large halos, but a study focused on a much larger number of collisions involving smaller subhalos to derive more general constraints on the self-interaction cross-section.  This was achieved by simulating self-interacting dark matter in galaxy clusters with various mass ranges and self-interaction cross-section profiles that matched actual galaxy clusters in observations.  These simulations showed that while strong self-interactions can reduce density at collision sites, this effect is reversed during subsequent collisions and results in increased density buildup over time.  This led to the formation of smaller, more dense sub-subhalos in a loop of accretion and coalescence that varied depending on self-interaction strength.  However, self-interactions also triggered the loss of subhalo structures, reduced orbital radii, and led to a shorter time to coalescence for subhalos, regardless of mass or density.  Furthermore, self-interactions caused subhalos to lose mass as they collided with larger halos and left behind minor gravitational lensing effects that increased with self-interaction strength, reached a peak coalescence time, and then diminished the subhalo mass.  This resulted in a predictable pattern in anomalous lensing effects that varied depending on the relative masses of colliding halos.  This study derived constraints for self-interacting dark matter that ruled out certain self-interaction parameters, especially for small halo collisions with self-interaction cross-sections across various collision energy ranges.  It also resulted in a two-fold increase in the viable parameter space for colliding galaxy-scale objects with self-interacting dark matter, especially for cases involving smaller halos and higher impact parameters, but with further research required to refine these results and better understand self-interacting dark matter. Autonomous Component Analysis is a feature extraction technique that operates independently, without supervision, utilizing a constraint on the rank of the data's covariance matrix. A modified version of ACA, referred to as M-ar-K-Fast ACA, has been developed, which provides an entry-by-entry update of the singular values and matrix factorization, offering faster computation and reduced memory requirements. Compared to ACA, M-ar-K-Fast ACA requires less time and computational resources, with improved scalability for large datasets. In addition, M-ar-K-Fast ACA's closed-form update allows for simplified implementation and reduced overhead. Two cost functions, penalizing rank and based on the trace of the nuclear norm, have been derived for M-ar-K-Fast ACA, with all necessary updates and implementations provided in a MATLAB package. The algorithm's convergence is guaranteed under specified conditions, with the optimal sparse solution being the hermitian transpose of the last column of the transformed data, normalized by its length. This makes M-ar-K-Fast ACA suitable for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and data visualization. Furthermore, M-ar-K-Fast ACA can be adapted into an online version for processing streaming data in real-time. The algorithm's efficiency and usability have been validated through a series of numerical experiments using datasets such as MNIST, Wikipedia, Twitter, stock prices, face images, and EEG signals, with the computational results providing novel insights. For instance, M-ar-K-Fast ACA has achieved competitive accuracy with deep learning on the MNIST dataset, while its online version can successfully classify Twitter posts and accurately predict stock price movements. The algorithm's developments and computational findings in this study are expected to contribute to the advancement of data analysis, machine learning, and artificial intelligence.
