We analyze a signal recovery method for complex, multi-dimensional signals observed under quadratic conditions. The standard approach for this task involves a mathematical optimization problem which becomes increasingly computationally intensive as the signal dimensions increase. To mitigate this limitation, we examine an efficient algorithm derived from this optimization problem and evaluate its performance. Specifically, we demonstrate the necessary and sufficient conditions for the signal to be recovered exactly. Furthermore, we show that with certain signal patterns, the signal can be recovered even when the signal dimensions are much higher. The algorithm's efficiency is illustrated by lower bound estimates of the number of observations required for recovery, which we calculate for specific signal patterns. Finally, we validate the signal recovery algorithm's performance through the results of simulations. The findings of this study indicate that the signal recovery algorithm is capable of handling high signal dimensions, which makes it suitable for applications such as magnetic resonance imaging. Historical approaches primarily utilize geometric estimation and a priori knowledge to tackle this problem, but due to LiDAR's limited view angles and undetermined pose parameters, this method is prone to inaccuracies and losses.  In contrast, neural network-based perception models that directly project data into a unified format have been shown to maintain better continuity, although this approach often necessitates per-device, per-model fine-tuning and is characterized by poor robustness.  This paper presents a novel LiDAR-camera integration framework called BEVFusion, which addresses these challenges by featuring a simple and robust architecture that adapts to various LiDAR camera configurations and performs effective data fusion with high consistency.  Its results are benchmarked against state-of-the-art models and demonstrate superior performance, while its source code is made accessible for public use.  Furthermore, this paper analyzes and attributes LiDAR's limited view angles to hardware and firmware factors and proposes LiDAR-based auto-detection and auto-compensation methods to improve its performance and ultimately achieves a 50% reduction in the error margin.  These LiDAR compensation methods may also find application in other directions, particularly in compensation for distortion caused by the presence of obstacles.  The integration of this technique and our integration framework, once fully developed, has the potential to yield very good results in real-life scenarios. This integration technique has the potential to augment a variety of perception capabilities and in particular the development of a unified representation of the environment from the two different modalities. This is supported by the finding that the minimal thermal disturbance in this regime exhibits the characteristics of a random Gaussian process with a hyperbolic tangent potential. This identification of the thermal disturbance leads to two key conclusions regarding the statistical properties of turbulent flows in the dissipation range. Firstly, the distibution of the vertical velocity component is asymmetric due to the influence of thermal fluctuations. Secondly, the interplay between the thermal disturbance and the fluid's kinetic motion causes a shift in the critical decay temperature of the thermal distribution from zero to a finite value. The value of the finite temperature is proportional to the square of the average energy contained per degree of freedom within the dissipation range. This shifted critical decay temperature indicates that at finite temperatures, thermal fluctuations are unable to isolate themselves from the turbulent fluid motion within the dissipation range. As a result, thermal disturbances are unable to exhibit critical decay behavior at finite temperatures within this regime. In contrast, the thermal disturbance is known to exhibit critical decay behavior at temperatures that far exceed those found in common experimental settings, a property that has led to the widespread assumption that thermal fluctuations are negligible in hydrodynamic fluid motion. In reality, the thermal disturbance is simply not the primary factor driving fluid motion in typical experimental conditions. In order to observe the pure thermal distribution, it is necessary to create a experiment or situation where the thermal fluctuations either drive the fluid motion or are the primary motion generators. Such experiments have been performed and have successfully demonstrated the predicted characteristics of the thermal disturbance in the turbulent state. In particular, the predicted characteristics were verified in experiments regarding lateral excitation forces and the backscatter spectrum. Consequently, the thermal disturbance is believed to be a ubiquitous property that appears throughout all scales where fluid motion is driven by thermal processes, a property that may be observed in both the dissipation range and the inertial range of turbulent flows. In 2012, a study discovered that liquid jets exhibit self-induced diffraction patterns resulting from the refraction of laser light by thermal gradients created by the laser itself. Our research aims to provide a in-depth analysis and expansion of that study, enabling more precise identification of the underlying physical processes responsible for the observed patterns. Our simulations reveal that the phase difference between light waves scattered at different angles is primarily caused by the average thermal gradient rather than the actual temperature difference. Additionally, we have derived mathematical expressions for the intensity and phase profiles of the scattered light, which may be used in future research to directly compare numerical simulations to physical measurements. Our simulations also identify a previously overlooked phenomenon where multiple, complex beat patterns can arise from the interaction between multiple laser beams. Our method involves calculating the modulus of the complex wavefront to obtain the intensity of the scattered light, as demonstrated in our 3D numerical illustrations. Our research confirms the experimental observations from the referenced study, and our predicted results are presented in a contour map showing varying intensity patterns across different thermal gradients. Our simulations reveal the relative contributions of two key processes - thermal expansion and diffusion of the liquid - which modify the phase profile and thereby induce or suppress the observed diffraction patterns. Our research confirms that the observed patterns are not a result of liquid refractive index nonlinearity but rather self-induced diffraction resulting from the refraction of laser light by thermal gradients in the liquid jet. The associate production of top and bottom quarks via the singular photon-quark connection has drawn attention from the scientific community due to its potential to significantly correct traditional Born predictions and provide insights into high-energy photon structure functions. This research presents phenomenological analyses of several non-resonant processes - neutralino pair production, $b\bar{b}W^+)$ creation and $b\bar{b}H$ generation - at the HL-LHC and the ILC, focusing on the singular cross-section fraction. It reveals that in hadron colliders, about 13% to 100% of total cross-sections can be attributed to the singular term, depending on the specific process and photon momentum fraction. This is significantly higher than at the ILC, where the singular contribution ranges from 2% to 35%. Crucially, in all cases, the singular terms exhibit negligible dependence on the relevant parameters. Furthermore, despite the lack of resonance in neutralino pair production and $b\bar{b}W^+)$ creation, resonant techniques still outperform phenomenological analyses, whereas in $b\bar{b}H$ generation, a different story emerges, with phenomenological analyses showing better performance at lower CKM matrices. To bridge this gap, we suggest using a new distribution that can differentiate between various photon structure functions at the HL-LHC, regardless of the specific photon momentum fraction. Finally, we provide a mathematical representation of the singular cross-sections in certain processes and propose using $b\bar{b}H$ generation data to determine the CKM matrix element $V_{tb}$. Machine learning models, particularly large language models like GPT-3, have shown the capacity to execute complex tasks envisioned for artificial intelligence, yet frequently produce responses that are perceived as inaccurately or irrationally pertinent by humans. The discrepancy between human and machine reasoning is particularly evident in scenarios involving intense modifications to visual content, where both humans and the GPT-3 model generate responses syndromatic of imagination, according to the results of a newly designed human subject study. The investigation reveals that machines are more likely than humans of perceive altered and unaltered scenarios equally, whereas humans show a greater distinction between them. The discrepancy between human and machine thinking is explored further using principles from cognitive science and the psychology of imagination, suggesting that cognitive shortcuts known as theory of mind in humans are responsible for this disparity in cognition. The findings of this study highlight the limitations of the current generation of AI models, which often excel in computational tasks but frequently fail in understanding the underlying human-based context of the task at hand. Recent breakthroughs in Zero-shot Natural Language Inference (Zs-NLI) are largely attributed to improvements in language models. This research investigates data-independent methods for enhancing model performance through prompt engineering. We apply transductive prompt design to the entire Zs-NLI dataset, varying prompt words and fixed label codes to achieve optimal results. Moreover, since choosing subwords in the prompt is subject to system-dependent constraints, we propose a method to assemble and rank dataset-subsets and prompt-combinations, then meta-tune the model using this new approach. This enables us to exploit variations of language models, enriches the training data, and achieves higher accuracy. We implement this method across multiple Zs-NLI datasets and observe significant performance enhancements, rising from 85.11 to 87.64 on the average Zs-NLI accuracy score. This method is notable as it produces high-quality results despite being independent of the underlying data. Upon examination, we discover that the Zs-NLI accuracy improvements result from the precise extraction of subtle word meanings, accomplishment of fine-grained semantics, and avoidance of misleading ambiguities. The code and associated models for this research have been made publicly available at https://github.com/ResearchInsightsAdvancingEducation/RIAE/blob/main/Zs-NLI_RIAE.py. This incorporation of RIAE is enabled by the use of the HuggingFace Transformers library, available at https://huggingface.co/transformers. We anticipate that this technology will have far-reaching applications in educational settings, ultimately benefiting all levels of formal and non-formal instruction. We intend for the RIAE framework to facilitate a greater understanding, work within the intersection of NLP and Education, and foster the incorporation of ML into education. We envision its extended incorporation to include the generation of educational materials, like lessons and instructional plans, as well as its use in discovering and learning new word meanings. We have used Monte Carlo computing to analyze the properties of an S=1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice, particularly its transition dynamics after symmetry disruption and in its liquid state. For two methods of symmetry disruption, we observed similar behavior: as the symmetry was fully restored, the disruption first triggered a spin wave gap then multiple domain walls. This suggests the possibility that the restored order may pass through an incommensurate nematic stage. In the liquid state without symmetry disruption, we found that the power-law decay of certain lattice quantities is weakened when symmetry is disrupted, but this does not seem to affect the decay of other quantities. This suggests the possibility that the expected superfluid transition in the undisturbed lattice may not occur if the symmetry is first destroyed. Conversely, the observed behavior suggests the possibility that the superfluid transition and incommensurate nematic transition may be the same phase transition, with the superfluid being highly resistant to changes in the network. Surprisingly, state-of-the-art models for interpreting language are not able to explain their outputs in terms that make sense to humans, unless they are finely tuned with large amounts of text, specifically trained on tasks and datasets curated by humans. Researchers have developed systems capable of understanding word meanings in relation to their context, but these systems are not able to accommodate sentences of any complexity and were not designed with human understanding in mind. Our work, on the other hand, involves creating a new language interpreter that can provide straightforward explanations, even with minimal training data, and can easily be trained on text, including social media posts, articles, and websites, along with relevant human explanations. By using examples of words used in specific contexts along with explanations of their meanings, our system is able to provide explanations that make sense in a natural way. Importantly, our system is able to understand meanings that are not found in training data and generalize its explanations in a way that is not based on statistical patterns. Our system is evaluated using multiple datasets and is found to provide accurate and natural-sounding explanations that are comparable to recent approaches. The Electron-Ion Collider, a forthcoming particle accelerator, is scheduled to deliver valuable insights into the fundamental components of matter by meeting the needs of nuclear physicists for in-depth analysis. A crucial component of the EIC's design involves the use of sophisticated devices to track the path of particles produced in the collider's experimental zones. Due to the high interaction rates and intense particle flux at the collider, these tracking devices must be capable of precise measurement and durable performance in challenging conditions. Engineered to meet this requirement, advanced silicon sensors have emerged as the preferred choice to form the central detector's spatial resolution framework. This article details the ongoing development of silicon sensor technology for the collider, with a particular focus on the ongoing fabrication process and testing of prototype sensors, specifically a double-layer sensor designed for the collider's common apparatus, the SoLID. This prototype consists of a forward-looking layer with 50 um and 300 um pixel widths, offering thin, heavy ionization loss measurement capabilities in multiple dimensions. A thorough characterization of this sensor's electrical properties, including data from a high-irradiation test, is performed using specialized tools and devices. Additionally, the most recent results from a radiation damage test of this sensor are shared, obtained via beam delivery at the Jefferson Lab's Accelerator facility. This test involved exposing the sensor to a high-energy beam, simulating the expected conditions of the collider, and then measuring its performance in terms of charged particle collection, residual frame noise, and other key factors for accurate tracking. Finally, a discussion of the sensor's manufacturing progress is presented, including discussions of design trade-offs and plans for the sensor's future version based on the expertise gained from this prototype. This expertise includes the sensor's logical arrangement, design specifications for its individual components, and the process of matching the sensor to its accompanying readout chip, with a particular focus on the development of a low-budget, high-efficiency system of silicon sensors and associated readout components for widespread use in the collider's common apparatus. A forthcoming system of this type, the Low Energy Electron Detector, is particularly significant in this regard. A detailed description of its design progress and findings from the ongoing development and testing of this component are presented. This device is particularly noteworthy for its ability to detect individual electron impacts with 50 fC sensitivity while offering a large detection area and extremely low material volume to deliver low-energy and single-electron detection capabilities. Observations of H30$\alpha$ radio recombination lines from NGC 5253, a low-metallicity galaxy, suggest the presence of star-forming regions producing fast-moving stellar winds and supernovae remnants. Analysis of these observations' intensity patterns indicates a variety of star-forming regions. However, the size of the observed complex in NGC 5253 exceeds the diameter expected for gas-driven winds and supernovae. The discrepancy can be explained by the effects of stellar winds and supernovae originating from low-mass stars, which consistently demonstrate smaller sizes compared to the observed value. In recent years, a deep understanding of Kerr-lens mode-locking has been achieved through advanced mathematical and computational methods, enabling researchers to precisely calculate and accurately simulate the phenomenon. This has particular significance in solid-state laser machines that produce short, powerful pulses at high energy levels. When these lasers operate near their longitudinal mode frequencies, a complex interplay occurs between electrical current, lasing pulses, and the medium in which the current is applied, resulting in an intricate description that includes mathematical models of nonlinear interactions, number theory, and wave physics. To tackle this complexity, researchers have developed reliable numerical methods that can be used to make precise predictions about KLML pulse behavior, including their growth, interactions, and eventual spectrum analysis. This has far-reaching applications in a range of laser technologies that produce extremely short, high-energy pulses for various scientific and engineering purposes. Several examples and demonstrations of KLML behavior in diverse contexts are presented. Future research is expected to focus on high-fidelity, three-dimensional simulations of KLML that incorporate advanced numerical techniques and could lead to significant performance improvements in next-generation pulse lasers. Simulations of KLML in an Yb:SiO2 chip laser are presented as an example of such future work. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of KLML theory and simulation for researchers and engineers working with high-energy, high-speed lasers, with a particular focus on numerical methods and related topics that are central to advanced laser technology development. Several open-source software packages and related projects are referenced. Suggestions for future research are provided at the end of the document. Research into the relationship between social media use and depression has been hindered by limited access to large datasets, prompting a need for extensive, annotated collections of online posts.  This research addresses this need by gathering and analyzing a large dataset of Twitter posts from individuals who have been diagnosed with depression.  By applying a machine learning frameworks to the dataset, we were able to identify patterns in the language and behavior used by Twitter users with depression, and explore their potential applicability to the detection of depression in online posts.  Importantly, our findings highlight the need for greater empathy and understanding in the language used to describe depression on social media.  This research sets the stage for the development of novel, machine learning-based interventions designed to combat depression among social media users.  Ultimately, our goal is to identify new approaches to depression detection and treatment, and to understand their potential value in the development of personalized, human-centered therapies for social media platform developers. The system in question consists of an applied force, its natural slope angle, and a frictional coefficient, with the system's descent either prevented or not, resulting in two distinct states: stick or slip states. The findings suggest that a system without obstacles can operate at a sustained, oscillation-free state with both types of feedback control systems, whereas a system without obstacles can only achieve convergence under velocity feedback control when its descent is not prevented. Reinforcement learning exploits the Bellman equation to design optimal policies in uncertain environments. However, the conventional approach to using a uniform discount factor faces challenges, particularly as tasks require varying levels of epistemic and aleatory uncertainties. According to the literature, choosing the wrong discount rate can result in inconsistent transitions between exploration and exploitation. This problem is rooted in the absence of a clear distinction between uncertainty types. A new model, called Profound Bellman Risk, introduces a probabilistic discount rate for each state in the Markov chain, directly addressing uncertainty within the Bellman equation. It uses a conservative model that preserves optimality and allows the state visitation distribution to influence the discount rates, thereby balancing exploration and exploitation based on the distribution. This improves reinforcement learning agents' performance across tasks with diverse levels of uncertainties. Experimental results show that PB Risk consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving stable breakthroughs in DQN, offline reinforcement learning, and Bayesian reinforcement learning applications. For instance, PB Risk yields up to a 30% reduction in the average time to the peak reward in the Classic Control benchmark, and up to a 5% gain in the Kornia benchmark compared to other improved variants. A detailed explanation and the associated code are available at a public repository. Personalized recommendation systems continue to dominate web platforms, remaining at the forefront of technical advancements. One essential component of these systems is sequential recommendation, which has seen significant improvements in recent years. Although existing research has extensively examined user behavior, a crucial aspect still needs attention - the explicit and implicit intentions behind user actions. In many cases, users have specific goals in mind when interacting with recommended content, although these goals often go unreported. Understanding user intentions would provide valuable insights for accurately modeling user behavior and guiding decision-making in high-stakes scenarios. This study proposes a comprehensive framework to uncover user intentions in implicit feedback datasets. Our research focuses on sequential user interactions in a real-world context, aiming to discern the underlying intent behind user actions. Our findings indicate that intent-driven models yield better performance compared to baseline methods and synthetic datasets with varied levels of intent ambiguity. Our framework can be applied to other recommendation datasets, yielding more informed user models and intention-aware recommendations. Additionally, our framework offers modularity, allowing users to select components based on their specific needs. This framework expands the scope of recommendation research, enabling the development of more sophisticated intent-aware systems. The search for rare $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ decays at colliders and in beam-dump experiments seeks to constrain New Physics beyond the Standard Model.  A semi-inclusive version of the latter has been proposed to improve sensitivity by reducing a crucial parameter, the $b\to s$ helicity strength. By removing SM contributions from inclusive $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ processes, a new variable, $R_{\rm sfl}$, is introduced, which remains sensitive to those parameters. It is emulated here with Monte Carlo simulations based on the $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ process, specifically using the LHCb detector conditions. As a result, $R_{\rm sfl}$ can be directly linked to the $\ell^+\ell^-$ polarization asymmetry and its sensitivity to New Physics is comparable to that of the standard, fully-inclusive $R_{D^\pm}$ and $R_{K^\pm}$ ratios. Consequently, this $R_{\rm sfl}$ variable offers a fresh opportunity for detecting New Physics beyond the SM, particularly in the $b\to (c,\,u)\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions. This paper presents a novel approach to regulating multiple-channel networks through decentralized methods that use local information in nodes to create adaptive controllers. By formalizing feedback channels as undirected and weighted graphs, a Cyclic Relative Entropy Minimization (CReM) problem is formulated, enabling a decentralized online optimization process to be developed for channel optimization. Unconstrained optimizations are performed by nodes, with gradient Descent-Newton methods used to iteratively optimize and converge on an centralized objective. In the limit, distributed algorithms converge to channel state estimates, which can be used to calculate the optimal gain matrices for adaptive controllers, enabling efficient regulation of linear networks. Simulations demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of the proposed algorithms, achieving convergence in as little as half the time required by the existing Distributed Newton Method (DNM) with the added benefit of plug-and-play capabilities and robustness to channel disruptions. Furthermore, the approaches presented require minimal communication, processing power, and rely on local measurements, making them suitable for large-scale complex systems and harsh environments. This paper also explores the feasibility of these algorithms in real-world applications by modifying a commercial multi-channel system used for sale in the aircraft industry to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms in practical settings. Finally, the approaches presented enable nodes to accurately estimate and regulate the movement of the human gait, enabling the development of prosthetic devices with a higher level of accuracy and reliability. By evaluating and testing the proposed algorithms on a variety of applications and systems, the approaches presented can be considered highly effective and reliable. The research community has been working to combat the COVID-19 pandemic since its inception, and a key aspect of managing the outbreak involves categorizing cases into infectious and non-infectious categories to mitigate spread and mortality. Existing methods, including clinical diagnosis and temperature screening, are flawed and fail to provide reliable and comprehensive data. A recent deep learning model, BERT, has garnered significant attention for its accuracy and efficiency, and we propose combining it with a two-phase model to optimize results. Our approach involves the use of multi-modal inputs, including medical history, temperature, and BERT attributes such as age, to categorize cases and eliminate information bias. A dataset of 890 cases with detailed clinical histories and BERT attributes was used to train the model, and our results show a competitive performance compared to existing models, including a high F1 score of 0.903 for predicting temperature and fatal outcomes. Our approach, and its associated code and dataset, has been made publicly available on GitHub through the repository COVID19-BERT. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of the two-phase model in optimizing outcomes, and the use of BERT attributes to mitigate information bias and provide accurate results. Additionally, our approach highlights the benefits of using multi-modal inputs in optimizing model performance and generalizability. Finally, the usability and reproducibility of the model have been ensured through detailed guidance and technical requirements. A new benchmark dataset with 1068 cases and precise labels has been used to evaluate against several current models, and our results show that the two-phase model can significantly improve overall performance and generalizability in real-world applications. Specifically, the model achieves improved F1 scores of 0.903, 0.799, and 0.035 for predicting temperature, fatal outcomes, and age in two-phase models, and its performance outperforms existing models, including a recent transformer model, and its results are available without human involvement. Additionally, the model's actual F1 score for temperature is 0.903, which is a boost of 0.135 compared to the best existing model, and our results are robust against various temperatures. A subsequent study has been conducted to evaluate the performance of the two-phase model on new datasets from different medical sources, and our results show that the model achieves generalizability by accurately categorizing cases from different data sources, and its performance is beneficial in real-world medical settings. This guide is intended for researchers new to the field of network research, offering a comprehensive overview of the subject and pointing them towards relevant resources for further study. Network analysis is an interdisciplinary field which has become increasingly significant over the past 20 years due to the expanding internet and the rise of big data in various fields. However, network research is a diverse and sprawling field with numerous methods and applications, making it inaccessible to newcomers. Our goal is to provide an entry point, familiarizing readers with the subject and guiding them towards key resources for deeper exploration. We focus specifically on the conceptual framework of the subject, examining the underlying structures that make up a network and the statistical methods used to analyze them. We also highlight important publications, databases, software tools, and professional networks that support researchers, as well as the core networks and organizations responsible for the development of the field. We cover the existing bodies of research, identifying the key research areas and presenting an overview of the state of the field as of 2020. Finally, we suggest opportunities for further study and exploration. We present this guide as a resource for up-and-coming researchers, particularly PhD students and postdocs, in the field of network research. Although it will necessarily be dated as of 2020, we intend for it to remain a useful entry point for the field, even in future. We envision that the guide will be of use to a broader community, extending beyond researchers to students, practitioners and professionals seeking to understand the field of network research. We have also included a companion document that provides a detailed guide on how to conduct network research itself. Our objective is to make this guide widely available and to continuously update it for the benefit of the network research community. An earlier version of this guide was initially created for the PhD students in the NetworKit research group at the Imperial College London. We have now expanded the guide for a broader audience and the read-only community can be accessed via https://networkscience.tutorial.rtfd.io/. A printed version of the guide can be accessed via https://networkscience.tutorial.printaura.com/. A video tutorial can be accessed via https://networkscience.lms.imperial.ac.uk/. Furthermore, the materials for the Linear Algebra and Graphs course, the Network Science course and the Data Science in Networks course are available via https://graphclasses.imperial.ac.uk/, https://networkscience.imperial.ac.uk/ and https://networkdata.imperial.ac.uk/ respectively. Achieving optimal model balance is crucial for both speech learning and representation tasks. While over-emphasizing speech learning might lead to poor representation quality, underwhelming task interest can similarly hinder performance. To explore this balance point, we examine the antagonistic relationship between two critical aspects of self-supervised speech education: speech model quality and teacher embedding quality. Using a two-stage approach, we initially identify the fundamental trade-offs associated with each task and then develop a specific training protocol that exploits these opposing effects in a iterative process, boosting performance on both tasks simultaneously. The resulting training procedure, dubbed Counterbalanced Pre-Training (CoPt), demonstrates consistent improvements over standard approaches, as evidenced by experiments on both LibriSpeech and LibriTSD. Additionally, our analysis provides fresh insights into the resources required to achieve a balanced state in self-supervised speech education. The source code and pre-trained models supporting our findings are publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, our research has significant implications for resource allocation in speech education, prompting a hypothesis that varying resource distributions can produce distinct outcomes. To investigate this idea, we identify and represent points of interest on a Pareto front, creating a decision-making tool to aid practitioners in CoPt applications. The interactive decision-making tool is also publicly accessible on our GitHub repository. The results of our study indicate that the CoPt strategy is successfully generalized to multiple counterbalanced training ideas, providing a framework for finding the optimal trade-off between speech learning and representation tasks. In a finite regular category, a subset Y of an object X can be visualized as a "superset" if for every subset X of X that includes Y, there exists a corresponding superset Y of X such that Y is contained within X. This condition can be represented as a preorder on the power set P(X), which consists of all possible subsets of X. However, for this representation to work, P(X) must be contained within the category. In such a case, a "superrelation" functor can be defined from the preorder (P(X)) to the power preorder [X, X], which represents all equivalence relations on X. This functor assigns to each subset Y of X, with its preorder [Y, Y] in P(X), an equivalence relation [X, Y] in [X, Z]. This leads to the establishment of a bicategory equivalence relation [X, Z] that corresponds to a preorder [Y, Z] in P(X), with the condition that Z is a reflective object in the category. In a finite category, a "superrelation" equivalence [X, Z] in P(X) can be characterized as a "distributive" superrelation if for every subset Y of X, the inclusion map Y to X distributes over the equivalence [X, Z], which corresponds to a certain universal property in a bicategorical framework. In a distributive superrelation [X, Z], a "symmetric and reflexive" partial equivalence relation [X, Z] in P(X) can be defined and serves as an equivalence connection in the category. This corresponds to a mathematical concept called an equivalence relationator in a bicategorical setting. In a distributive superrelation [X, Z], its reflexive and symmetric version can be extended to a symmetric and reflexive superrelation [X, Z]' in P(X) such that [X, Z] is contained within [X, Z]'. However, the superrelation [X, Z] serving as a factorization of [X, Z]' is not considered here, but rather a reflexive and symmetric version [X, Z] of an equivalence connection in the category, which can be obtained after removing its non-reflexive part from [X, Z]'. This leads to the establishment of a "superspace" functor from the category's regular preorder to the category's regular bicategory equivalence relations, with the equivalence connection [X, Z] serving as a "superrelation" functor from the preorder to the bicategory.

Currently, the largest CLIP models contain more than 1 billion parameters but still can not perfectly understand human vision, leaving room for further development. This research proposes new training methods for CLIP models to enhance their performance. These methods involve incorporating multi-modal input to improve model capacity and refine contrastive learning with contextual operators to raise quality. Additionally, a pre-training dataset called VT-CLIP, comprising 240M fine-grained image-text pairs with extensive context, is introduced to provide guidance during the CLIP training process. When applied to image-text retrieval, our approach, based on the mid-scale ViViT-VL5, achieves an accuracy of 88.8% on the flowery dataset, surpassing the current best result of 87.1%. We also integrate our model with different object detection frameworks, such as Faster-RCNN and EfficientDet, and further improve the overall performance, with improvements of 3.0% and 2.4% achieved on the Image-Net dataset, respectively. In the era of Expansive Data, the task of working with data grows more unwieldy. As our understanding of biological sciences transforms into a data-driven framework, managing an enormous amount of genetic information becomes particularly problematic. A novel method of reducing our DNA sequence-based database into a compact, interpretable space has been developed. The proposed framework begins by training a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to automatically classify non-biotic sequences without any supervision, subsequently utilizing the hard embeddings derived from this process to extract features in a Soft Attention block. The resulting cycle enables our MLP to learn a unified, low-dimensional representation of DNA sequences, thereby enhancing the accuracy of our classifier and surpassing the performance of traditional feature engineering methods. The presented research demonstrates the feasibility of using hard embeddings derived from unsupervised neural networks as effective molecular descriptors in place of traditional feature engineering techniques. Furthermore, the proposed method can be integrated into numerous unsupervised word embedding techniques for sequence encoding. The compact, low-dimensional representation learned by our DNA sequence-based database can be employed for diverse bioinformatics applications. The presented research includes comprehensive experiments to validate the efficacy of the proposed method in contrast to other techniques. The proposed method was implemented in TensorFlow and is available through our GitHub repository for other researchers to replicate and build upon. The expected accuracy of the proposed method was assessed using GRP as the benchmark to set a baseline for evaluating its effectiveness. The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 97.65% in classifying random DNA sequences, 83.81% for classifying ChIP-seq binding predictions, 99.90% for classifying protein-ligand binding affinity predictions, 70.19% for classifying cancer classification tasks, 71.68% for classifying chemotherapy response predictions, and 65.25% for classifying breast cancer subtypes. In the current battle against COVID-19, using CT scans to diagnose the disease has emerged as a crucial measure. To supplement limited hospital resources, we developed an innovative solution - a remotely workable web platform that enables automatic COVID-19 detection from CT images. Building on the capabilities of capsule networks, we designed a sophisticated model to achieve superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art models, especially when dealing with rare diseases where partial samples are common. Our two-stage network effectively rectifies the challenges posed by partial and noisy scans, demonstrating superior performance on both single-image and ensemble detection tasks. To further facilitate global COVID-19 detection, we translated our model into a lightweight, device-compatible web version, reducing latency and enhancing user experience. Using a dataset of 10,579 low-dose CT images, we tested and evaluated our model's performance, ultimately achieving a high AUROC of 0.95 for the best-performing configuration. Explainable AI techniques are essential for understanding how recommended products are chosen, including which factors influence user preferences and how specific interactions shape product rankings. Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations - Recommender Systems (LIME-RS) is a method that enables the evaluation of tabular data-based recommendation systems. However, LIME-RS has been found to sometimes produce inconsistent or unstable interpretations, which raises concerns about its reliability. In an effort to address these issues, we first seek to identify cases where LIME-RS may overfit to small, random fluctuations in training data. We also aim to provide a measurable indicator of LIME-RS stability that can help compare the reliability of different models. Utilizing a publicly available dataset from MovieLens, our results suggest that LIME-RS's instability is often the result of weak or missing constraints in recommendation systems. We also demonstrate that LIME-RS's performance can be improved by applying domain knowledge to these constraints. Finally, our results indicate that LIME-RS's quality of interpretation is correlated with its predictive accuracy, but this correlation does not necessarily guarantee the model's actual reliability. Consequently, users of LIME-RS should be aware that the method's interpretations are not always reliable and should consider applying additional constraints to small, random datasets to ensure the model's trustworthiness. The provided code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/nyu-joey/2020-Misc-LIME-RS. Compliance and Stability in LIME-RS Interpretations for Recommendation Systems was presented at the 2020 ACM Conference on Information and Knowledge Management. This density adjustment aims to achieve a one-dimensional electron system for magnetoelectronic device applications, with a calculated surface electron g-factor of -1.2 for the high density state. However, due to the initial presence of oxygen-related defects and poor surface quality, the InAs quantum well is found to be pinned at the Fermi level by these defects. Multiple processes, including laser annealing, halide solvent atomic layer deposition, and an Al$_{0.8}$GaS$_x$ overlayer growth are combined to remove these defects, thereby achieving a well-behaved high-density state in the InAs quantum well. With a well-beaved high-density state, the interplay between the Fe$_3$GaTe$_2$ ferromagnetism and the surface quantum well electrons can be studied and utilized for the implementation of magnetoelectronics. Nonetheless, the challenge of achieving a well-integrated high-density electron system at the surface of these materials, as posed by their initial non-ideal characteristics and the imperfections in their surface layers, needs to be addressed through a combination of these sophisticated growth techniques and a tailored removal of surface defects. Achieving learning resilience often involves using robust regression models that
can handle out-of-distribution inputs, including regional data with unique
characteristics not found in the training dataset. Unlike regular learning, 
regionally inspired methods utilize separate models for different areas or 
datasets to prevent failures of all models when faced with novel inputs. The 
key to this approach lies in gradient alignment - a mechanism allowing models 
trained on similar regions to converge numerically even when model parameters 
do not match. Two practical implementations of this concept have been successfully 
applied in industry settings: (i) two-stream training, and (ii) multi-domain 
learning. The fundamental question remains, though: how to choose which regions 
to use. Our study answers this query by showing that using regional data 
corresponding to the distribution of training labels aids in learning resilience, 
while proposing a quantitative framework for this purpose. Our analysis is 
supported by theoretical and empirical evidence, the latter being based on 
experiments with CIFAR, ImageNet, and TN-CSV datasets. Additionally, a produced 
pytorch library, available on our website, enables users to implement regional 
inspired learning methods for images and speech datasets. The website also 
provides a deployed AWS instance for users to test the implementations. The 
code is accessible at https://github.com/kundajelab/regionally-inspired-learning. 
Lastly, an associated video illustrates the study using ImageNet datasets; the 
video can be viewed at https://youtu.be/4R8p2UoP2Qs. The study is further 
documented in a paper whose details are available at https://arxiv.org/weakly-supervised-learning. 
Even though the study is wide-ranging, our focus here is on obtaining a 
geo-spatial overview of the data to determine the beneficial regions for 
regional-inspired learning methods. The study demonstrates that by learning in 
areas with similar distributions to the test dataset, we can achieve a high 
probability of sample success. Consequently, our approach yields a simple 
metric - Kullback-Leibler divergence - to identify the useful regions for

In the drag approach to radiation phenomena, the behavior of charged particles interacting with charged and neutral substances is analyzed in terms of a particle's acceleration due to radiation pressure. This process is considered a universal effect applicable to fields of space, laboratory particle beams, and accelerator environments. The interaction between the particle and substrate is characterized by the particle's acceleration, with the substrate's response determined by its resistivity. Three distinct scenarios are explored, including the cases of elastic, inelastic, and photon-induced interactions. The latter scenario gives rise to the Compton effect, which is used as a reference point to establish a universal distance between the particle and substrate. This distance, denoted as $d_0$, is calculated based on the Bohr radius for elastic interactions and the electron Compton wavelength for inelastic interactions. The drag approach is further refined by incorporating the effect of radiation drag in quarks, which is analogous to the phenomena observed in the Pound-Rebka effect and the SLAC electron-positron collision experiment. Additionally, the drag principle is applied to the semiconductors Si and GaAs and the superconductors Nb and Y, with the observation that at a certain distance, the drag acceleration exceeds the escape velocity of the particle, resulting in a trapped particle trajectory. A comparative study of the drag effect in various materials reveals that materials with lower electron mobility exhibit stronger drag within a shorter distance from the substrate, while materials with higher electron mobility allow for trapping at a larger distance. Furthermore, the drag effect in superconductors is found to have a finite distance of validity, beyond which the drag acceleration becomes negligible due to the limited mean free path of the electrons. A novel invention, the resistive substrate, is also proposed as a device that can trap and confine particles at a distance from its surface, with the potential for a range of applications. The method and principle of designing such a device are also outlined, which is capable of confining both charged and neutral particles. The process of creating the device involves introducing a metal layer on a semiconductor substrate, with the direction of the metal layer purposefully considered to determine the polarisation of the electron gas on the substrate, relative to the surface of the layer. This device can trap particles at a distance from its surface, with the distance determined by the thickness of the metal layer and the material used as the substrate. The polarisation of the electron gas on the substrate is achieved through this device design and requires the device to be oriented in a specific way to determine the axis of the particle trajectory

We have established that the solutions to the HS equation exhibit Lipschitz robustness, utilizing an extension of the recent method developed by Venkatesh and Visinger. The primary challenge in this instance lies in the unbounded nature of the Riemannian curvature, which necessitates the incorporation of novel control mechanisms to ensure curvature is within defined, finite bounds. We have solved this problem by integrating the ideas of Bang and Wang, incorporating affine transformations, and defining a new type of control function based on distance metrics. As a result, our paper contributes to the body of work involving robustness by providing the first demonstration of Lipschitz robustness for the HS equation, as well as extending the concept of minimal solution solutions. Furthermore, our methods have significant implications for the integration of HS equation solutions into the development of rugged integrable equations. The final section of our paper involves an application of our findings to the more general context of minimal surface problems. As an example, we have demonstrated the existence of rugged XIX equations. We anticipate that our methods will facilitate the discovery of other robust equations in the future. The paper concludes by previewing future research directions. The proof of its central result spans 6 singularly distinct cases over 34 individual proof sections. The proliferation of semantic segmentation algorithms exploiting Convolutional Neural Networks highlights the irreparable value of annotated data in improving model performance. Nonetheless, the accuracy of manual annotations is susceptible to inter-observer variability and artistic decisions, leading to potential errors and inconsistencies. Consequently, the development of methods to counter label noise is essential to rectifying noisy labels and drawing attention to misclassified samples, thereby facilitating the efficient correction and optimization of annotated data. This study introduces the Bayesian Analytics Guided Label Restoration Mechanism, an innovative approach utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks and Bayesian analytics to rectify label noise through a regression-based method. By employing a shallow neural network to predict pixel-wise regression labels based on the Sigmoid activation function and incorporating category-wise normalization, the label restoration model is able to effectively rectify label noise across various datasets, including the well-known CIFAR-10 and CheXpert datasets. Furthermore, the label restoration method is able to improve the robustness of medical image categorization tasks by counteracting label noise, as exemplified by the model's performance on the CheXpert dataset and the CIFAR-100 dataset. The relationships between the training and testing phases of our experiment are explored and analyzed, along with the effects of varying size and language on the accuracy of our results. The outcomes of our study demonstrate that hate-speech identification using a well-established model trained on a large English dataset is effective for both Hindi and Bengali classification tasks, while also showing that a translation-based approach yields higher hate-speech identification rates than using a model trained exclusively on Hindi and Bengali datasets. The combination of these techniques provides the best results, leading to the possibility of developing a powerful, large-scale hate-speech identification model that can be applied to multiple Indian languages, specifically Hindi, Bengali, and English. The potential applications of our study are expansive, allowing our results to be used in a variety of real-world scenarios, such as social media monitoring and forensic investigations. The present study and its outcomes contribute to the following research areas: hate-speech identification, neural networks, translation, and identification processes for Hindi and Bengali languages on social media platforms in India. In space exploration, detecting nuclear collisions with the surface of celestial bodies is crucial for understanding the history of impacts. High-resolution chambers may be able to identify these collisions, but this ability is hindered by a variable depth of detection that affects the accuracy of location measurements. One method for enhancing detection capabilities involves utilizing information about kinetic energy and recoil direction. By analyzing data from a 50 micron thick silicon chamber, we found that incorporating this information can boost the size of the area where collisions are likely to occur by a factor of 25. The mesoscopic approach, which considers multiple pixel hits as part of a larger area, can also help distinguish true events from accidental coincidences. By applying this approach to a proposed layer of detectors on the Orion spacecraft, we found that it can decrease the likelihood of incorrect detections caused by chance coincidences, particularly in the center of the recoil-sensitive area. Consequently, it is feasible to achieve a high detection rate and minimal loss in the measurement of location measurements for recoil-sensitive chambers. Moreover, it is possible to design a chamber that is sensitive to recoil and can be used to identify the location of impacts on lunar and other celestial bodies, such as Earth's moon. The above findings were published in a paper for the Lunar Science Conference 2021, specifically in a session about the future of nuclear science on Earth and in space. This paper reports on the winning entry from the 2022 Out-of-Lexicon Semantic
Reranking Challenge held by the University of Cambridge. A comprehensive
challenge task involves generating pairs of phrases with similar meanings,
given a reference phrase, a query phrase, and a list of candidate phrases.
Evaluations are based on the accuracy of the highest-ranked semantic equivalent
in the output, and the model must also perform well across a wide range of
domains, including law, medicine, and others. To achieve a high score in this
challenge, our solution utilized a pre-trained Transformer model, combined with
a two-stage approach that incorporates a combination of full sentence and phrase
pre-training, and leverages pre-trained masked LM features to produce the
semantically richest candidates at the top of the list. Additionally, our solution
utilized a combination of dense and retrieval-based ranking methods to produce the
final result, and we achieved a final score of 83.96 on the official evaluation
dataset with our best hyperparameter configuration. More details about our approach
are available in a publicly-viewable GitHub repository.

The Fr\'echet distance, a measure of signal similarity, offers a well-established alternative to traditional measures. However, it lacks the triangle inequality property, which poses difficulties for indexing, leading researchers to investigate approximate nearest neighbor search algorithms that can compensate for this limitation. These algorithms can provide a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation to the Fr\'echet distance in $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1})$ time, depending on the parameter $\epsilon$. Recent studies have focused on reducing the time complexity, but a theoretical lower bound of $\Omega(\epsilon^{-1})$ remains, leaving the optimization problem with an open question: what is the minimum number of operations needed to achieve the $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation? To address this, we propose a modified version of the lossy Cope-Dudnik-Rotikov (CDR) index, applying it to time sequences, which yields a more efficient approximate neighbor search algorithm for the Fr\'echet distance with a lower bound close to $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}\log{\epsilon^{-1}})$. Additionally, we proved the modified CDR index satisfies the range property, offering a more flexible search algorithm with the potential to improve performance. Our results contribute to a more accurate understanding of the performance limitations of approximate neighbor search algorithms, with the computational analysis providing valuable insights into the trade-offs between time and query complexity. Furthermore, we prove the lower bound of $\Omega(\epsilon^{-1})$ holds even when using a range of standard indices, such as balls trees and k-d trees. With the ability to achieve the same $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation in $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{2}\log{\epsilon^{-1}})$ time using a traditional index, the efficiency gain of our proposed algorithm is significant when dealing with very small $\epsilon$ values. Similarly, the computational analysis indicates our proposed algorithm is much faster than the naive search algorithm on very small $\epsilon$ values before the benefits of the modified CDR index are overshadowed by the negative effects. To facilitate future work, we list all the lower bounds known at the time of our research in the appendix, hoping to contribute to a theory of the costs and bounds of approximate neighbor search algorithms. To address this issue, we have developed a scalable solution to provide accurate scores and mitigate assessment errors. The proposed approach uses Bayesian inference to iteratively select students for additional rounds of assessment, ensuring that all students can complete an unlimited number of extra assessments. The method exhibits optimal performance by minimizing total assessment count while maintaining accurate score estimation. The Bayesian iterative selection technique can be combined with various scoring methods, such as beta-binomial or deep learning models. We have tested our approach with a scoring model, demonstrating that it accurately reproduces a scoring system's performance while offering a substantial reduction in the number of assessments required to achieve similar accuracy. The code for this proposal is available on GitHub at https://github.com/mentalhq/scale. For individuals who are unfamiliar with a place's layout, effectively navigating can be challenging. One common method to overcome this is by creating mental maps, however, individuals who are not expert map navigators face another difficulty which is translating their mental maps into action. This study focuses on solving this problem by developing HiTMap, a universal topological map representation which simplifies the layout of a space into the configuration of interconnected nodes and edges. In comparison to standard map diagrams, HiTMap's structure is more efficient, allowing it to be reduced into a compact format known as the Minimal D-Graph. By utilizing the D-Graph format, navigators can record their route details and refer to them as needed, and also use it to guide their navigation with the aid of a Path Navigation System, which suggests the most convenient sequence of turns. The study also involves a practical evaluation of the idea through the development of a mobile app called HiTMap, which is designed to assist individuals who are not expert map navigators, especially those with visual impairments, in providing improved navigation assistance. The app allows its users to create a user-friendly space map, record the route details, and also use the app to guide their navigation. A user trial was conducted to assess the efficacy of the HiTMap representation and the Path Navigation System as a whole. The study's key findings indicate that HiTMap provides an enhanced and efficient diagram structure, and the Path Navigation System is user-friendly and accurate. It is our hope that HiTMap could be a useful aid for various purposes such as a mobile app navigation system, a universal storage format, and a potential inspiration for a range of applications in cognitive science, human-computer interaction, and related fields. In this study, we examine the problem of context-based Named Entity Recognition (BER), a more complex task than standard name entity extraction as it requires identifying the context in which each extracted name is encountered. BER is particularly relevant to scenarios such as reconstructing articles, where previous mentions of entities need to be connected to their corresponding contexts. We investigate various approaches for retrieving the context in which an extracted name is encountered and assess their efficiency on the book graphs dataset. We then combine the most effective context retrieval methods and evaluate their performance on the berdataset, a BER dataset comprised of articles and their associated metadata. Notably, our approach leads to significantly improved F1 scores of 8.1 and 10.3 points for the base model and BERT with masked language modeling, respectively, when considering the top 16 term retrievals. While numerous research studies have concentrated on analyzing structured and formally designed text, such as specifications written in a specific language, we investigate the inverse problem: extracting software requirements from general, unrestricted human language. To accomplish this, we create a software application called SpecSearch. SpecSearch employs a diverse set of technological tools, including a pre-trained, extensively trained language model, a specialized search algorithm, and a rule-based system to identify and interconnect related concepts within a large database containing numerous definitions. In recent years, many surveillance and monitoring systems have been established in diverse settings and are now requiring real-time data transmission from remote locations.  Achieving real-time data transmission from these locations often requires a substantial number of wireless transmitters, which results in significant operational costs, both in terms of energy consumption and equipment maintenance.  To minimize these costs, we are exploring more efficient approaches to data transmission.  In this study, we present a novel model that combines device scheduling, relay selection, and network coding for real-time data transmission.  The model also incorporates a solution for energy-efficient network encoding.  Previous research had identified the incompatibility between real-time data transmission and network coding, which had necessitated a considerable amount of feedback.  To resolve this, we have developed a coding scheme that can transmit multiple encoded messages simultaneously.  By using this scheme, the requirement for feedback is significantly reduced.  A novel time-slotted encoding scheme is also presented to optimize network encoding efficiency across the network.  The study also incorporates a solution for joint relay selection and network encoding.  The solutions for scheduling, relay selection, and network coding are formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem in an effort to minimize energy consumption and equipment usage.  The problem is first converted into an equivalent dual problem and then formulated as a network flow problem that can be efficiently solved using simplex method.  A set of synthetic data is used to validate the proposed solutions.  The solutions are shown to significantly reduce energy consumption and equipment usage while maintaining real-time data transmission requirements.  The optimal solutions for the problem are shown to range from 66.79% to 87.01% and 61.09% to 85.35% respectively in terms of decreased energy consumption and relay usage when compared to traditional solutions.  The corresponding throughput increase is shown to be between 61.09% and 66.79%.  The time complexity of the proposed solutions is shown to be a function of the number of devices, relays, and data packets, and is reported as O(m*n*(k+1)) where m is the number of time slots, n is the number of devices, and k is the number of data packets.  The time required to solve the problem using the dual approach is shown to be highly dependent on the problem itself and is advised to be improved using a more efficient algorithm or by formulating the problem as a linear programming problem. This paper introduces a groundbreaking framework that interprets the local structural and energetic state of a disordered, high-energy excited solid. By redefining the mathematical approach to nonlinear NEXAFS phenomena, we have developed a more sophisticated rate equation that better captures the complex multi-step electronic transitions within the system. By expanding upon the initial theory, we have significantly increased its practical utility, allowing the equation to be adapted and applied to various symmetries in the final state. Recent advances in machine learning have been successful in training systems to perform this task, but these systems become less effective when applied to scans from different clinics due to variations in image processing techniques. To address this limitation, we explored two approaches: training a machine learning model to adapt to new data over time and teaching a model to handle the differences in data from various clinics. We found that adapting a model to new data is more effective and leads to better outcomes, and we identified the key factors contributing to this success. Moreover, we discovered that the accuracy of a model is closely linked to the quality of its training annotations, which we also evaluated. These findings are expected to inspire further research on improving the accuracy of Multiple Sclerosis lesion segmentation across different clinics and data sets. Various studies have demonstrated that statistical neural-network (NN) force-field estimations often deviate from actual trajectories. In the past, these discrepancies have been addressed using general methods such as regularization and error minimization, but their underlying causes remain unclear. In this study, we employ the adjoint method to determine the source of NN errors in dynamical systems. By utilizing the adjoint solution, which represents the optimal, opposite trajectory that maximizes NN errors, we demonstrate that these errors result from a combination of two factors - model inaccuracies and force estimation ambiguities. Both parameters can be estimated through the adjoint solution's derivative with respect to unknown parameters. As the adjoint solution uniquely determines NN errors, even without force data, this approach allows for the quantification of model inaccuracies using experimental force data. By incorporating force data, we can further determine NN errors' direction. This study validates the proposed algorithm using both analytical and numerical methods on a single-degree-of-freedom example and extends it to three-degree-of-freedom cases. Its applicability to various applications is also explored. The final version of this work is published at arXiv:2209.09363. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a method to reduce the computational cost involved and proved its effectiveness on datasets such as IMDB, SST-2, and CoQA, achieving near-optimal performance compared to full-tuning and outperforming current best practices. The method to reduce computational cost involves the simultaneous adjustment of parameters while keeping the weights of large-scale models unchanged, which also improves memory efficiency. The method also includes a novel technique called Unique Token Adaptation, which utilizes a set of token-wise vectors to complement the capability of pre-trained models in handling unique words. The method can be used on various tasks, including classification, question-answer matching, and more, and can be accessed via the open-source repository https://github.com/ericliwen/UEPA. Understanding the process of glass formation is crucial, but a major obstacle lies in the lack of a well-defined theoretical explanation.
This study presents a new approach by analyzing the correlations between the thermodynamic properties of static glasses and specific dynamic characteristics observed using nuclear inelastic scattering, a technique that enables direct observation of local dynamics in liquids.
For polymer liquids, a strong link was discovered between the stored energy and the complexity of the local structures, with certain dynamics causing frustration and increasing the likelihood of glass formation.
This relationship holds true even when accounting for system variations in molecular weight, chemical composition, and external pressure.
These findings demonstrate that a well-defined correlation exists between static and dynamic thermodynamics, which can be utilized to forecast the onset of glass formation.
This knowledge may lead to the development of strategies for preventing glass formation, for example by introducing dynamics that reduce frustration and increase the mobility of molecules. Furthermore, this approach may be applicable to a broader range of materials. Nonetheless, the process of forming liquids is even more complex. Hence, the idea that a direct correlation might exist between the stability of liquids and remote atomic arrangements remains unverified. Nonetheless, analyzing the links between static and dynamic thermodynamics and nonlocal structures may reveal new insights into the nature of glass formation. This study offers preliminary evidence establishing a direct correlation between the stability of liquids and remote atomic arrangements in a specific context. Further research is required to obtain detailed nonlocal descriptions of glass-forming liquids. Such a study may be feasible using techniques like molecular dynamics simulation or nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. For instance, we have shown that a molecular dynamics simulation can be utilized to forecast the onset of glass formation based on the correlation observed in a glassy alloy. Importantly, the approach is applicable to a range of materials with minor modifications, and the forecast can be based on the correlation observed in a different system. Hence, the method holds potential for being utilized widely across materials. Nevertheless, the method's validity depends on the existence of a well-defined correlation between the static and dynamic thermodynamics, as observed in the polymer liquids. Expert analysts provide in-depth commentary on neural network decisions by pinpointing crucial areas within an input image. By examining how they focus on specific features, we can gain insight into the processes underlying expert analysis. Nevertheless, existing methods that attempt to replicate this commentary through attention mechanisms fall short, as they do not accurately capture experts' focused areas. This failure is largely due to the fact that, during explanation, analysts typically don't just provide a brief summary of the input, but instead, they focus on making something new, such as creating a meaningful object within an irrelevant image. Building upon this understanding, we have formulated a novel method that not only accounts for where experts focus, but also what they focus on. By incorporating look-ahead prediction, our method generates more accurate attention maps by taking into account the semantic meaning of the desired focus areas. As a result, it significantly outperforms previous best practices. Moreover, our method allows for the creation of tailored models that can mimic this commentary by incorporating both visual and linguistic information. By leveraging these models along with the generated attention maps, analysts can gain a deeper understanding of the processes underlying expert analysis. There's no perfect algorithm for creating summaries, and even seasoned professionals may struggle with specific sections of a document. Finding the ideal summarizer, especially for intricate subjects like microbiology, can be like finding a needle in a haystack. Platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk offer a vast pool of workers with varied levels of expertise, allowing researchers to conduct experiments that reveal the advantages of collaborating with specialized individuals, even in the face of potential biases associated with seasoned professionals' handcrafted summaries. By  1) utilizing search terms to identify Turkers with relevant knowledge, 2) creating a training set comprising summaries created by experts and novice summarizers, and 3) comparing the performance of a neural network and ensemble methods on a test set consisting of documents related to microbiology and other fields, we're able to highlight the significance of collaborating with specialized individuals and provide insights that may guide the design of future workflows that leverage MTurk in a more efficient manner. Furthermore, our analysis also provides valuable general insights that could potentially apply to other applications of automated summarization. Davis has proposed a novel method to measure the recoil proton polarization in deep inelastic ep scattering, making the ds/dt differential cross-section section more distinctive from non-relativistic kinetic factors. By implementing this method along with traditional variables such as F2 and the generalized structure function 2, the Davis variable offers significant insights into the partonic processes involved in DVCS. As a partonic-independent variable, the Davis variable is particularly valuable in understanding the long-range nature of quark-glue correlations in small-x phenomena. We present analytical calculations of the one-loop level for Davis and demonstrate that it can serve as a crucial test for achieving full saturation of the Bjorken sum rule for gluon distribution throughout the accessible range of x < 0.21. To facilitate experimental research on Davis, we outline a viable detection approach using a hybrid technique combining the CLAS and HPS experiments, achieving a precise resolution of ds/dt of 10-14 GeV^2/c^2. Our research indicates that achieving a ds/dt resolution of 10-15 GeV^2/c^2 is feasible with specialized electron beam polarization techniques. We provide a detailed comparison of the analytical cross-sections of the Davis variable in the kinematic range of DVCS, as well as its descriptions within the leading-order parton model, QCD factorization, and saturation models. By enabling distinct measurements of the Davis variable at various facilities, including the proposed MESA and EIC experiments, across four distinct kinematic ranges, the concept of recoil proton polarization in DVCS offers significant theoretical advancements and enables novel experimental investigations. This study presents a theoretical assessment of the direct and parasitic beam-induced background impacts on signal measurements in muon colliders. Specifically, we examine the background generated by full-intensity muon beams, damping rings, and muon injection/extracted systems. We also investigate the effectiveness of various beam manipulation strategies for reducing this background. Notably, we conclude that by employing a 'anti-signal' beam, it is possible to eliminate direct background signals. This achievement, however, relies on the approximate cancellation of induced background muons at the interaction point. In cases where this cancellation is not possible, the 'anti-signal' beam reduces the background only partially. The remaining background can be further minimized using a beam spreading technique, though this method does not entirely eliminate the background. In addition to these strategies, we found that utilizing a low-emittance, high-energy muon injection beam could offer a potential reduction of the background. Nevertheless, this strategy requires further investigation and validation through particle accelerator simulations to confirm its feasibility. Ultimately, a combination of these beam manipulation techniques may be necessary to achieve a sufficiently low background level to ensure the accuracy and sensitivity of the Higgs boson measurements at the ILC and the muon collider. Such a low background would be a prerequisite to enable the measurement of rare interactions between muons and the Higgs boson. In cases where this requirement is difficult to meet, the measurement of the Higgs-rho interaction would become inaccessible. In summary, our research indicates that various beam manipulation techniques are available to reduce the beam-induced background at these future colliders; nonetheless, further study into the technical feasibility of these strategies is necessary to ensure these methods can be applied in practice. Creating models that reduce neural network overcapacity by encouraging sparsity
in neural network outputs is an important aspect of creating efficient and
interpretable neural networks. However, implementing a meaningful definition of
sparseness that lends itself to differentiable training has been an obstacle until
now. We present an innovative approach called differentiable sparseness, achieved
by formulating sparseness as a optimization problem and using the assignment
cost to define a ratio. The resulting objective function leads to a new
framework of sparse differentiable models that can be easily extended with new
optimization techniques, allowing the application of vector routing and gradient
explosion techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by
achieving significant sparsity in state-of-the-art models for reinforcement learning
and self-supervised learning. Additionally, our framework allows the training of
large neural networks on GPU. We validate the effectiveness of our framework in
reducing the memory usage of neural networks by up to 30%. Our framework is
available at https://github.com/ruishiwu/differentiable-sparseness.

The current method of sparseness is poorly defined as it relies on the
    non-linear activation function's zero threshold. Our framework addresses this
    issue by assigning each output j a zero-contribution value of z_j and
    enforcing activation z_j only on the j-th dimension. We adopt the
    assignment-cost approach for a novel framework of sparseness that can be
    trained with various optimization techniques. Each dimension j has a value
    z_j, either 0 or 1, and our framework applies a differentiable regularization
    R_f, via the Wasserstein regulation R_f(z) = ||z_f - z||_2^2, to enforce
    assignment. The resulting framework allows the training of neural networks
    with a multi-objective optimizer, and our experiments show that the
    assignment-cost approach achieves better results than existing methods. Our
    framework achieves state-of-the-art sparse results in state-of-the-art
    models for reinforcement learning and self-supervised learning. Notably, our
    framework reduces the memory usage of the powerful Vision Transformer of
    local CPU and GPU by up to 30%. Our framework is available at
